#4164. Review: Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered (Switch 2) - The King Returns With A Fun But Thin Kaiju Brawler

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered

Godzilla fans are eating well. At the time of writing, we are on the brink of a new Toho release, a direct sequel to Goji’s first Oscar-nominated film, Minus One. There's also the next entry in Legendary's MonsterVerse to sate fans of the Western arm of the franchise (even though they have been a little Kong-heavy of late). Now, Tokusatsu mayhem is coming back to consoles, as original developer Pipeworks and Atari revamp their 2002 GameCube classic Destroy All Monsters. It smashes its way onto Switch 2 with Unreal Engine 5 visuals, online multiplayer, and some nice quality-of-life bonuses.

Destroy All Monsters Melee is a 3D arena fighter where you can choose from 12 iconic (well, maybe not Orga) kaiju and duke it out in major cities across the globe. It's an absolute joy to play for fans of the franchise, and it's accessible enough that anyone can jump in and relish the city-trampling mayhem.

There is a thin wraparound story that, while patently ridiculous, is in keeping with the lunacy of the series' Japanese entries. An alien race called the Vortaak has invaded Earth, unleashed the inhabitants of Monster Island and taken control of the kaiju that come pouring out. You play as the one friendly monster that has to battle their way to the alien mothership and take on the Vortaak's cybernetic facsimile of Earth's mightiest monster - Mechagodzilla.

That's the overarching plot, and there's only a tiny sliver of story across a couple of cinematics in the game's Adventure Mode, so don't expect a rich narrative. This game is mostly monster fights, and in this respect, it does not disappoint.

There really isn't much more to be said about the joyous spectacle of hefting Gigan over your head and hurling him into the side of a skyscraper. You can fill Anguiris with a faceful of atomic breath or fly rings around your opponent as Rodan. Destroy All Monsters Melee is filled with these moments of wonder amidst what is a fairly straightforward brawler. There are no elaborate combos here, no precise hitboxes, and no need for frame counting. There’s just multiple building-sized animals wailing on each other.

Each monster has basic punch and kick combos, coupled with powerful variants triggered by a push of the right stick. A power move knocks enemies flying at the cost of speed (Godzilla's tail whip is overpowered on any difficulty), while projectile abilities help manage distance.

Monsters can also enter Rage Mode, which lets them unleash a powerful ability that comes with an impressive visual flourish. Power-ups litter the arenas, sometimes dropped by the Vortaak’s 1950s-style UFOs. These will either top up health and special meters, or send in Mothra for an aerial bombardment. When in doubt, you can always pick up a building and throw it at your opponent.

Each monster gets its own distinct moveset, and the uniformity of the controls means it's easy to try out everyone before you settle on a main character. Godzilla is a good all-rounder, and his Millennium model is the best-looking in the game. Gigan has a powerful teleport ability that can easily bamboozle an opponent. Several monsters can fly, with Mecha-King Ghidorah in particular being a formidable combo of offence and evasion.

There are some duds, like Megalon and Orga, who have utility but just don't feel great to play. I had the most fun with Mechagodzilla (here depicted in his Heisei Kiryu form for the remaster), who combines his Maser Cannon projectile with shoulder-mounted missile salvos.

Single-player offerings include the story-driven Adventure mode, which comes in three tiers of difficulty. Survival mode has you run a gauntlet and try to last as long as possible. For pure brainless wish fulfilment, there's Destruction mode, in which one or more kaiju lay waste to a city to rack up points.

There's also a full suite of local and online multiplayer modes, including a tournament ladder to decide once and for all who gets to be crowned king of the monsters. Monsters level up in the Adventure Mode, increasing base stats and adding abilities to their repertoire, which incentivises spending time with each fighter.

The system for unlocking new arenas and monsters, which involves repeating fights in the local modes, has been updated for this remaster. Previously, the ‘research’ tied to specific unlocks was fixed. Now you can freely choose which one you want to prioritise (pro tip: unlock Ghidorah first).

That said, there isn't much to do beyond the final bit of research, and getting 100% is a patience-testing loop of the same old fights. The magic of this game is in the pick-up-and-play nature of those battles, and it doesn't stand up to laborious repetition just to view some nice artwork.

The presentation of this remaster on Switch 2 is exemplary. Monster models and arenas have all been updated, and battles play out butter-smooth both docked and undocked. Undocked in particular looks great, with those big chunky fighters and diorama cityscapes really suited to portable play. There's a real fluidity to some of the action, particularly when monsters like Gigan close the distance with incredible speed.

The audio combines lovingly polished sound effects from the movies with a cacophony of city-levelling bangs and garbled military transmissions. It's a real shame there isn't Japanese vocal audio; the early-2000s English voices really take a layer of authenticity away.

Special mention must go to Director mode, an enhanced photo mode that lets you control the camera during a fight. Adjusting the speed and setting up the perfect shot of your favourite beasts laying into each other is addictive fun. You can see why Ishiro Honda made so many of these movies.

Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a satisfyingly faithful update to a beloved Kaiju brawler. It’s simple and fun, with local and online multiplayer keeping you around for the long haul despite a wafer-thin single-player experience. Now if we could just get a remaster of Save The Earth and Unleashed…

#4163. "We made a very difficult decision": Australian indie showcase Freeplay reject antisemitism claims after delisting a Jewish sponsor who was allegedly accused of being a "zionist"

Unnamed speaker criticised Unpacking dev's inclusion

The organisers of Australian independent games showcase Parallels have rejected accusations of "prejudice" and say they've received "violent threats", after a Jewish developer had her sponsorship of the event refunded. The developer in question is Wren Brier, creative director at Witch Beam. She claims an unnamed speaker booked for the event has accused her of being a "zionist", following an article about her work from an Australian Jewish publication.

On 8th October, Brier announced that Parallels organisers Freeplay had refunded and delisted her sponsorship, following complaints about her involvement from the anonymous speaker. According to Brier, the speaker called her a "zionist", apparently based on the presence of Witch Beam's 2021 puzzler Unpacking in a round-up of Israeli and Jewish-made videogames from The Jewish Independent, published on 5th October to mark this year's Melbourne International Games Week. Brier herself does not identify as Zionist and does not live in Israel, having left the country as a teenager.

There is much heated disagreement about what "Zionism" involves. Many protesters of Israel's vicious and inhuman war on Gaza define Zionism as a violent ethnonationalist project, comparable to European fascism, but the term has a long history that encompasses the desire for safety and security among Jewish people amid virulent antisemitism in other countries, before and after the Holocaust. I am not Jewish, and my understanding of these things is threadbare, but one thing we can say for sure is that being Jewish does not make you a Zionist. To conflate the two is actively antisemitic.

"I am Jewish," Brier wrote in her Bluesky thread from 8th October, which was posted a few hours before the Parallels event began. "I was born in Israel. I emigrated to Australia when I was 18. I did not serve in the military. I have never expressed any anti-Palestinian views. I really wanted to believe that 'zionist' wasn't a dogwhistle for 'Jewish' but I don't know what else it could be here.

"No one bothered to check whether the accusation was true," she went on. "The first I heard of any of this was this morning, when Freeplay told me they were refunding my donation and removing me as a sponsor because my mere name being listed 'has created an untenable environment' for their speakers."

Brier says she was not aware that Unpacking had been featured in the Jewish Independent piece. She credits the game's inclusion to the fact that it contains three Jewish cultural items - a dreidel, a menorah (pictured above on the table), and a hamsa, among hundreds of other objects the player is asked to unbox and arrange. "That was enough to make a speaker accuse me of being 'zionist', which in turn was enough for Freeplay to remove me as a sponsor, literally on the day of the event," Brier wrote.

"I've always loved Parallels, I've even participated in it myself and showed Unpacking there way back in 2018," she continued. "But I don't think I'll ever be able to support it or Freeplay again. I know at least one Freeplay board member has quit the board over this, too. This is discrimination, pure and simple."

Other game developers have come forward in Brier's support. "For the record, I had heard via-via murmurs of this and strongly objected to describing you as Zionist, and vouched for your person several times," wrote former Vlambeer co-founder Rami Ismail in response to her Bluesky thread. "I'm so sorry things played out like this. This is indeed deeply distressing."

Former Splash Damage writer Ed Stern added: "Wren, this is so stupid and absurd I don’t even know where to start."

Recently founded industry news site Vertical Slice have since obtained a copy of the email to Brier, informing her that her sponsorship had been refunded. "We value you as a member of the Freeplay community," it reads, "but unfortunately your involvement in Parallels has created an environment that is untenable for a number of our speakers, and it is very important to us that Parallels 2026 goes ahead. Freeplay has mixed feelings about this very difficult decision, and we sincerely wish our speakers had raised these concerns earlier so we could engage with you and look for a solution."

According to This Week In Videogames, meanwhile, two Freeplay board members in total have resigned over the decision to exclude Brier. TWIV further report that this year's Parallels event included several statements of support for Palestinians in Gaza, with addresses from Freeplay board member Joel Davidson and Origame Digital's Naphtali Faulkner, developer of the recent post-colonial horror Penguin Colony. Among the games featured at the event was Dreams on a Pillow, created by Palestinian developer Rasheed Abueideh, who was not present at the event, but recorded a video segment.

Supporters of Palestinians regularly call for a boycott of products made in Israel, and of projects or companies such as Microsoft that have business connections with the Israeli state and military. Unpacking does not appear to have any such links: according to Brier, it was made by developers based in Queensland, Australia, with funding from state body Screen Queensland. As for Brier's sponsorship of Parallels, she was not present at the event itself, but sent her studio logo for inclusion on the sponsor list.

Hitherto, Freeplay and Parallels have been affiliated with the Melbourne International Games Week, itself organised by the state cultural body the Australian Centre for the Moving Image. But according to a spokesperson, the ACMI "acted immediately to pause its support" after learning about Brier's delisting. “This was a clear breach of the Games Week code of conduct, which prohibits discrimination on any basis including sex, sexual orientation, gender, race, religion, disability, or any other protected attribute," the spokesperson told This Week In Videogames, noting that Freeplay are an independent entity and that they did not consult with the ACMI, before delisting Brier.

Now, finally, Freeplay themselves have come forward with a statement about the situation, which was sent to RPS among other outlets, following a request for comment yesterday. The statement doesn't identify the originator of the "zionism" claim.

"For 22 years, Freeplay has been a diverse, inclusive and welcoming place for people of many different backgrounds and perspectives to get together, chat about games and our lived experiences," it reads. "We can’t express how much we value our community, sponsors and donors and all of the support we have received over the years.

"Recently, the board decided to refund and remove acknowledgement of a donor from Parallels 2026," they go on. "The donor has been a valued member of the Freeplay community for many years. We regret the manner in which aspects of this process occurred and the upset this has caused within our community. We will be seeking further discussions with all affected parties to hopefully achieve a better outcome for the situation moving forward.

"The public discussion has included serious allegations about the motivations behind our actions," the statement acknowledges. "We reject suggestions that Freeplay acted out of prejudice towards any person or community. We made a very difficult decision under significant time pressure with the understanding that Parallels 2026 was at risk of not going ahead."

"We understand many of you would like clarity on the events from us," Freeplay write. "Given the sensitivities of the situation, and our responsibility to everyone involved, we won't be commenting on private communications or the various claims that have been made publicly. This week, members of our board have received violent threats, which we have reported to the police. We know that feelings in our community are running high. We ask that if you choose to engage online, please do so with care and respect for everyone involved."

#4162. Animal Crossing: New Horizons gets a new item to celebrate 25 years of the series

The allegedly finished game might finally, truly be feature complete with the addition of an anniversary item.

Animal Crossing: New Horizons has received a surprise patch today to celebrate the 25th anniversary of the life sim series. The update, version 3.0.2, is available across the Switch and Switch 2 versions of the game.

The patch brings a single new addition to New Horizons - a leaf item. Everyone gets it, too, so you don’t have to do anything special to acquire it.

After installing the patch, simply head to your in-house mailbox to claim it. The mail includes a hearty message to fans who supported the series for years, featuring an appropriate Nintendo N64 stamp.

The Leaf Statue, as it’s referred to in-game, lights up when placed.

April 14, 2011 marks the release of the original, lesser-known version of Animal Crossing in Japan. The game was initially released as Animal Forest (Dobutsu no Mori) on the Nintendo N64, before later making its way to the Nintendo GameCube in December of the same year as Dobutsu no Mori+ with some extra features.

That same, original design of the package is also available for display in your game. The rest of the patch notes are entirely about various bug fixes, so not much more there. You can see the full change log on Nintendo’s support website.

#4161. Yakuza Creator Toshiro Nagoshi's Studio Has Officially Shut Down, Ending Gang Of Dragon's Development With It

Nagoshi Studio, the developer led by Yakuza/Like a Dragon series creator Toshiro Nagoshi, has officially shut down, ending development of Gang of Dragon, which was revealed at The Game Awards last year. Shareholders resolved to dissolve the studio on October 31, according to a notice published in a Japanese government newspaper called Kanpo, as first reported by Gematsu.

This follows a report from Bloomberg earlier this year that said Chinese gaming megacorp NetEase Games was cutting funding to Nagoshi Studio, allowing Nagoshi to seek independent funding elsewhere. It seems he couldn't find funding, and now Nagoshi Studio is no more. NetEase helped Nagoshi found the studio in November 2021.

You can watch the Gang of Dragon reveal trailer below for a look at what the team was cooking up:

This closure follows other signals that NetEase is looking to divest from the gaming scene outside of its Chinese studios. A little over a month ago, Suda51's Grasshopper Manufacture left NetEase to go independent again, just months after the launch of Romeo Is A Dead Man.

#4159. Metro 2039 goes back to its Metro underground roots, with a story shaped by the war in Ukraine and the people who suffer it

Metro 2039 takes us back to the tunnels of the Moscow Metro where, fittingly, Nazi ideology never died.

The Metro series is finally, officially back with a new installment. 4A Games has just unveiled Metro 2039 to the world, the follow-up to the outstanding Metro Exodus, released all the way back in 2019.

2039 takes an unusual route with its scope, however. Rather than build on the semi-open-world structure of Exodus, the upcoming sequel instead brings the focus back to where it all began: the Metro.

What won’t be changing is the kind of game that it is. Metro 2039 remains, like its predecessors, a story-driven, single-player game. Returning to the confined spaces of the Moscow Metro brings the focus back to the claustrophobic, uneasy atmosphere of the original games.

The game’s protagonist is, for the first time, going to be voiced throughout. From what we’ve been able to see, the psychological horror in this installment will be driven more by the very real effects the apocalypse has had, and continues to have, on denizens of the Metro.

2039 has been in development for years, but 4A Games has been rocked by two considerable events: the 2020 Covid pandemic, and Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, where the developer is based. The game’s darker story has changed in response to that.

The team’s Ukrainian perspective is molded into the narrative, and more prominently represents the toll the events of the last several years has taken on members of the team, their families and communities.

According to the developer, you can expect a bigger emphasis on choice and consequence, with Russian author Dmitry Glukhovsky returning to co-write a narrative that explores the compromised morality of a post-war society.

The new protagonist’s return to the Metro comes with the reveal that the different underground factions are now united under one banner, the not-so-subtly named Novoreich. Lead by a former Spartan, the Novoreich is an authoritarian regime which offers what it believes to be the only path to salvation.

4A Games remains majority Ukrainian, with teams based in Kyiv, and Malta. Unlike most AAA projects today, the studio continues to rely on its own engine tech. The 4A Engine is given a major upgrade for 2039: ray tracing is now a core component of the rendering pipeline, but the tech has been rebuilt to run better on modern hardware.

Today’s reveal sadly didn’t feature much gameplay - only a brief first-look with a mix of gameplay and cinematics. The developer, however, emphasised that creating cluttered, believable and lived-in environments remains a key focus.

Metro 2039 is set for release sometime this winter on PC, Xbox Series X/S, and PS5.

#4158. Resident Evil makers Capcom reveal data breach has affected over 11 million Capcom ID accounts, warn against potential phishing emails

"Credit card information was not included among the affected information," say the publishers

Resident Evil, Street Fighter, and Monster Hunter publishers Capcom have revealed that a data breach has seen a third-party gain access to information associated with more than 11 million Capcom ID accounts. "Suspicious activity" around the service, required to play online in the likes of Street Fighter 6, was initially noticed on October 19th according to Capcom, who have spent the past couple of days taking measures to contain and combat the problem.

Capcom have outlined in a press release that a total of 11,774,247 accounts had their email addresses and "system-specific identifier information" accessed in the breach. 43 of those accounts also had their date of birth, gender, country/region, and nickname records accessed.

"Capcom has not confirmed any compromise of Capcom ID account login passwords originally set by customers themselves," the company wrote. "However, the company has confirmed that passwords were changed without authorisation on 196 accounts. The passwords associated with these accounts have already been reset, and the company continues to investigate the scope of any impact resulting from this incident. Going forward, Capcom will notify customers affected by this incident. Credit card information was not included among the affected information.

As for other advice to affected folks, Capcom issued the following warning regarding the possibility of phishing attacks directed at the email addresses exposed in the breach:

"Email addresses registered with Capcom ID may continue to be used without interruption. However, there is a possibility that the affected information could be misused to send fraudulent emails or other communications impersonating Capcom or related parties. If you receive any suspicious email or message, please exercise caution and refrain from accessing any URLs contained therein or opening any attached files."

Having reported the breach to Osaka's Prefectural Police and Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission as part of their initial response, which they say "identified and addressed the attack method involved in this incident", Capcom will now plough on with a "detailed investigation" designed to flag measures that might stop this sort of thing happening again in the future.

#4156. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Switch 2 Development Team Has Been Revealed

Nintendo has just released the first two parts of a new Ask the Developer series all about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2. Alongside a bunch of interesting insights about the game's development, the interview also finally reveals the development team behind it.

As it turns out, the Switch 2 remake was developed internally by Nintendo's Entertainment Planning & Development (EPD) Production Group No. 3 — the team that has handled just about every Zelda entry since the early 2000s.

The remake saw HokWai Ng take on the role of Director (his first Dir. role at the company, though he also worked on Tears of the Kingdom), with Aya Shida (Pikmin 3, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, Tears of the Kingdom) on Art Direction, Hiroki Taguchi (Breath of the Wild) as the Program Director, and Masato Ohashi (Animal Crossing: New Horizons, Splatoon 3 Expansion Pass) as Music Lead and one of the Sound Directors.

There was a part of us that thought Nintendo might bring in another studio to work on the remake — particularly as it increasingly appeared more and more faithful to the original — but it's nice to see that it was an inside job instead. Worry not, Zelda legends Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi both served as producers on the project.

Parts three and four of the OoT Ask the Developer series will be released tomorrow (3rd November), so we're sure that there are even more dev stories to come. Gosh, what a week to be a Zelda fan!

#4155. "It just seemed arbitrary, and not very smart": EA was never a responsible owner for Bioware, but the developer never seemed to learn from their mistakes

19 years after buying Bioware, Electronic Arts have closed the veteran RPG developer. But as saddening as this is, bringing an end to series such as Dragon Age and Mass Effect, EA have never had an easy relationship with the studio.

Looking through old interviews with developers who worked across Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age, Mass Effect, and Anthem, the corporation immediately changed the atmosphere of the studio and never seemed to understand what exactly they had bought, or even why.

However, another thread of the conversations is that from project to project, Bioware repeated the same mistakes, getting years into projects before working out what they were trying to make. Sometimes they could pull an exceptional game out of this mess, but other times it led to costly missteps like Anthem.

Back when I was running TechRadar Gaming, features editor Jeremy Peel worked with Jon Bailes to produce the oral history of Mass Effect. I'm hideously biased, but it's an excellent account of that game's development. It was during the RPG's creation that EA acquired Bioware, and developers on the game immediately noticed a change.

"What I noticed once EA came in was how the language changed at work, and started adopting more corporate-isms, like the language of corporate America," audio design lead Steve Sim recalled. "At one time if you needed help on a project, you'd say, 'I need more guys,' or 'I need more people to help me out with this.' And then it turned into, 'I need more resources.' So the biggest change I found was just the change in the language, especially amongst producers and that type of crowd. They were assimilating into the Borg, it seemed."

It's the kind of language that you will find through the open letter published by EA's chief operating officer David Tinson and chief studios officer Cam Weber. The first reference to Bioware's closure is tied up in the euphemism "Saying no to some things we're passionate about". Doing so, they say, "allows us to focus our teams and resources so we give our biggest opportunities everything they need to succeed."

Also speaking in the Mass Effect oral history, director of technology and Bioware co-founder Trent Oster describes the immediate costcutting EA enacted on taking over the studio. "When we were acquired we were all looking forward to it like, 'Yeah, we're owned by EA, they're going to give us a budget, we finally don't have to keep constraining ourselves and crushing things down and cutting corners.' And one of the first things they did was like, 'OK, based on your budgets, we need to cut across the company 10%.' And we were like, 'Oh, so we're not getting more, we're getting less.' That was a bit of the EA feeling. We call it the EA butter knife. It just seemed arbitrary, and not very smart."

The corporate cost cutting Oster describes took place nearly 20 years ago, but it continued throughout EA's ownership. Most recently, in 2023 when 50 staff were laid off to “shift [Bioware] towards a more agile and more focused studio”. Then in 2025, more staff were laid off, this time it was described as "taking [the] opportunity between full development cycles to reimagine how we work at BioWare".

It becomes particularly clear with Anthem, Bioware's launched-but-quickly-shuttered live-service game, how EA's influence manifested at the studio. Interviewed in the Summer Eternal Anthology, long-time Bioware writer David Gaider explains the design concept for the game seemed to be formed from executive demands. "The nearest I could tell, working in a corporate environment, was that it was a sifted-down list of bullet-point requirements, that no single person ever took responsibility for," Gaider explains. "It just kind of happened like that. There needs to be this project, so it was willed into existence, but nobody would say that before this project is actually kicked off, someone needs to take responsibility for the vision."

Mark Darrah echoes this in his own interview in the anthology. "Casey pitched the exact thing [EA execs] wanted to hear," he says. "Always online, live service, infinite revenue. Multiplayer." Darrah describes it as "a near-perfect pitch deck." But, he also questions whether "Bioware is the company to make a live service looter shooter."

However, while those ideas may have filtered down from EA and then been pitched back to them by Bioware leadership, it meant that work would begin on a project long before it had crystalised into a clear premise. "The idea was that they could kick the project off, and that the designer, the design department, or the creative director, particularly, would then create the vision," Gaider says. "But at that point, the project's already happening. So each time it felt like trying to catch a bronco bull who's already out and running and bucking, and you're just trying to keep up."

For that reason, Gaider claims "Anthem was doomed from the start."

Development on Anthem began in 2012, but when Gaider joined the project 18 months later, it was struggling. "The team on it was just going around in circles," Gaider says. They didn't know what they wanted." Hudson then left Bioware in 2014 and Darrah says "they basically ran with no leadership, for two, three years." In 2017 Hudson returned and Darrah was brought over from the team working on the next Dragon Age project. Over the next two years Anthem took shape before it eventually released in 2019, but, in doing so, it meant the Dragon Age team was also then left without leadership for the next two years.

"My biggest regret," Darrah says, "is I kind of feel like I should have told EA 'no' when they asked me to take over Anthem. I should have just let whatever was going to happen, happen at that point." He adds that leaving "Dragon Age running without an executive producer from 2017 to 2019 was bad. That was a huge mistake."

Darrah says he doesn't feel like he had a choice, however, because "EA was very good at making Bioware feel like things were very dire." Though, he points to the fact that Hudson's replacement as Bioware's general manager, Gary McKay, was able to delay Dragon Age: Veilguard through multiple financial years. "That tells me either he's magic, which is possible, or it was never quite as 'gun to our head' as we thought it was," Darrah says.

(Bear in mind Darrah was being interviwed ahead of Bioware's closure and he's referring to events in the past five years.)

However, while pressure from EA may have significantly impacted the development and direction of Bioware's games, it appears that the studio repeated the same mistake for decades. Gaider, Darrah, and the developers that contributed to the Mass Effect oral history, all say Bioware consistently got deep into projects without having a vision of what they were trying to build.

"When we started, Dragon Age's big premise was 'It's D&D, but it's not'," Gaider says in his Summer Eternal interview. "We'll just file the ID numbers enough to make it our own. We went through a long period of going around in circles on Dragon Age." Edwin's covered this as a push and pull between teams that thought they were making Conan, others thinking it was Lord of the Rings, and still others thinking they were making a new Diablo.

Gaider believes the only reason EA allowed Bioware to complete the original Dragon Age was because the team "were already halfway through development, and [EA] considered it sunk cost. They said, 'Well, you've got to finish this.' But it was clear that Electronic Arts considered Dragon Age, our initial vision, to be too old fashioned, too slow, and too ponderous."

Gaider says Mass Effect had the benefit of Casey Hudson, who was able to pull together a single vision for the project much sooner. Though this may be something of a grass is greener situation, because the developers on Mass Effect describe being on the game for three years before it started coming together and even then it was only because they had to prepare something for E3.

"It was the first time we pulled together playable moments in the engine that really proved to us what the game was capable of," Hudson says in the oral history. "Until you pull things together, it's all sort of theoretical, and you think you know what game you're making. But once you have that moment in time, where everything's pulled together, you know exactly what the game needs to be."

It was only after the vertical slice was completed, lead designer Preston Watamaniuk says, "that the team understood what we were building and was able to then work autonomously, without as much hands-on direction."

This approach continued through the years. In 2012 Bioware began work on Mass Effect: Andromeda. Three years into development they scrapped the plans and tech they were using to procedurally generate worlds switching to a more traditional style of RPG, making the bulk of the game in its final 18 months. In 2015 they started work on a their next Dragon Age project, which was shelved in 2017 in favour of the project that would become Veilguard, but that would then take another seven years to complete, with a live service component first adopted from Anthem and then dropped after Anthem's failure.

It looks to have still been a problem for the studio with its current Mass Effect project. First announced back in 2020, initially as part of the "N7 Day" and then followed up with a teaser trailer at The Game Awards, the new Mass Effect was still described in EA's open letter as in "early-development". Developers who worked on the cancelled game are saying they believe they were "making something special", and aimed build on what they saw coming out of Larian and CD Projekt Red, but six years is a long time to still be in early development and sounds a lot like the project could have fallen into the "going around in circles" Darrah described of Dragon Age and Anthem.

I am saddened by Bioware's closure. The team have put out incredible games over the decades, and it sounds like they were never a natural match for EA's executives or the corporation's goals. However, it also sounds like the studio have continued to face the same challenges on projects year after year without really learning how to avoid them.

Still, it would have been much better that they be allowed to spin off and become independent or be sold to another publisher who knows what the talented team can create, than to be closed down after years of staff layoffs and project cancellations.

#4154. Blizzard will talk about Diablo 4: Lord of Hatred one last time before the expansion's launch next week

We're well under two weeks from the launch of Diablo 4's next expansion, Lord of Hatred, but there's more yet to be said.

Diablo 4 is mere days away from the launch of its biggest expansion yet, and Blizzard wants to make sure it got one last chance to tell you about it. Lord of Hatred is the follow-up to 2024’s Vessel of Hatred, and it’s set to arrive on April 28.

Next week, however, we’re getting an updated look at the new content as part of a livestream. This is the Developer Update kind; the meaty, information-dense show anyone who follows Diablo’s livestreams should be familiar with.

The next Developer Update is set for Thursday, April 23. It’ll kick off at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 6pm GMT. The show will, naturally, focus on Lord of Hatred. In particular, we’re getting another look at the expansion content that hasn’t been given the same level of coverage as the bigger features.

Everyone knows about the new Skovos region, the Warlock class (and the Paladin before that), but we haven’t seen much from the other gameplay-altering features that affect a lot of the core flow.

In next week’s showcase, Blizzard will show off the updated and expanded skill trees - which come to all classes, the Talisman system, and the gear-altering Horadric Cube. War Plans, the new make-your-own-endgame feature will be discussed, too.

More interestingly, we’re also going to hear about the new season kicking off right alongside the launch of Lord of Hatred. A short, in-betweener season is currently live in Diablo 4, and it’s going to end right as the next one/the expansion launch.

And, of course, the show won’t end before the team takes a few questions from chat, as is tradition. If you want to catch it live, you’ll be able to do so on Diablo’s official YouTube, Twitch, Twitter, and TikTok channels.

#4152. Nintendo Wanted To Remake Ocarina Of Time To "Trigger New Insights" For Future Titles

"Hang on, why is Nintendo remaking Ocarina of Time again?" It's a natural question that might have occurred to you in the last few months, and in the latest Ask the Developer interview, Series Producer Eiji Aonuma had the answer.

Part of the reason for returning to the title, it turns out, was to try to "trigger new insights" from the developers that may feed into future Zelda games. "Many of the team members who work alongside me on Legend of Zelda games today have only experienced developing the more recent titles," Aonuma-san says. "That led me to wonder, 'Do they truly understand just how significant The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was to the series as a whole?'"

"I started to wonder how they'd interpret The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as they go about developing future Legend of Zelda games," he continues. "By learning the game structure and development style behind the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and by actually rebuilding it as a full remake, it may trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development."

While he describes the potential behind such insights as "extremely valuable," he also notes that it wasn't the only reason he wanted to return to OoT for the series' 40th anniversary. The game's structure is drastically different from more recent series entries like Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, two games that a whole generation of Zelda fans will have grown up on (as sobering a thought as that is), so Nintendo wanted to showcase a different style of gameplay, too:

In The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, part of the fun comes from progressing through a carefully paced adventure and story, gradually building up the player’s growth and their understanding of the narrative along the way. We wanted players who had grown accustomed to Legend of Zelda games like Breath of the Wild, where they can freely choose their own path from the start, to experience that kind of gameplay as well

Whether revisiting Ocarina of Time actually does influence any future games' design decisions remains to be seen, but if you're looking for GoodGameTM inspiration, it certainly isn't a bad place to start.

The Ask the Developer interview also revealed that Ocarina of Time was internally developed at Nintendo, with HokWai Ng in the Director's seat.

#4151. Xbox reportedly mandate four days a week in office for staff close to Microsoft's Washington HQ, up from three day requirement brought in last year

Change set to take effect from beginning of February next year, it's claimed

Xbox have reportedly informed staff that, from the start of February 2027, those within commuting distance of Microsoft's Washington base will have to come into the office four days a week. This follows the mandating of three days in office last year, and comes as the company are looking at cutting more staff as part of ongoing efforts to eventually get rid of 3200 people in multi-round mass layoffs.

"Starting February 1st, 2027, Xbox employees in Puget Sound who live within 50 commuting miles of Studio D are required to work from the office a minimum of four days a week," Xbox's chief people officer Jacinda Chislum Pearson wrote in an internal memo seen by The Verge.

Pearson continued that the company have "thousands of Xbox employees within commuting distance of Redmond" and couched the move as being about the idea that "working together in person makes it easier to review work, resolve issues, and make decisions without the burden of scheduling another meeting".

The Verge report that the switch to four days in office will only apply to staff deemed to live close enough to Microsoft's Redmond campus and cite the memo as suggesting "established in-office practices" at Xbox-owned studios won't change. Though, the site do note that Xbox staff who've already been given or agreed exemptions to Microsoft's previous return to office mandates will need to resubmit for them. Last September, Microsoft internally announced plans to bring in rules mandating staff within 50 miles of the Washington campus come into the office three days a week, with those rules coming into force in February of this year.

It doesn't take a genius to look at the situation and predict that Xbox staff seem likely to have a strong chance of getting a memo around this time next year demanding they prepare to begin commuting in all five days of the working week.

While this move might turn out to have been planned well in advance of Microsoft's current spate of layoffs and studio rejigging, it's not surprising to see a company reportedly planning to cut more people loose in the coming months pushing out new rules affecting how remaining staff have to go about their jobs. Make people's working lives less convenient and you make even those who were previously content more likely to seek opportunities elsewhere, if there are any decent ones to be had, or to just leave.

As of writing, Xbox parent company Microsoft are also still subject to a BDS movement boycott over their reported ties to the Israeli military.

#4150. The Sims 4's much maligned paid mods have made it to consoles, but Kits are coming back to PC

The Sims 4's Marketplace and user-created content have officially arrived on consoles, a little over a month after their debut on PC.

The Sims 4 players on PlayStation and Xbox have now caught up to their friends on PC, at least when it comes to the game’s Marketplace. This new feature is essentially a hub for paid mods and other user-created content.

As often happens when long-established games introduce paid mods, The Sims 4’s wasn’t especially well-received, in part because of the introduction of a new premium currency - Moola - that is the only way to purchase any of that content.

The Moola denominations and prices are similar to many other in-game currencies, and the criticism around them is the same: they obfuscate the true value of items, and because of the way those denominations are structured, you’ll never be able to buy exactly what you need.

For most games, the subject of paid mods has always been fraught, and that's certainly true for The Sims 4. In the announcement blog post, Maxis said that the launch on consoles will work similarly to what PC players have seen, in that Kits will no longer be available to buy directly with real money on the PlayStation and Microsoft Stores. While Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs will remain, you’ll need to buy Moola if you want to acquire Kits going forward.

Interestingly, however, EA seems to have changed its mind somewhat on the Kits situation. A recently leaked memo (via SimsCommunity), appears to show that the publisher intends on making Kits available for purchase directly again, without the need for Moola.

Unfortunately, this only appears to affect the PC version, with the reversion reportedly forthcoming on both the EA App as well as Steam. Indeed, according to the same report, the change has already taken place on the former, with the latter following on April 20.

Considering the Marketplace only just launched on consoles, the company may wait to see if the decision to remove Kits from console platform marketplaces will be as poorly received as it has been on PC.

If you’re looking to jump back into The Sims 4 to check out all the new paid content, make sure you’re well-equipped with our list of Sims 4 cheats and debug options, or this one specifically for the Royalty & Legacy expansion cheats.

#4149. Feature: Threads Of Time - The Best Ocarina References & Easter Eggs In The Wider Zelda Series

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a masterpiece. An enduring classic that set the standard, and often the template, for virtually every single action-adventure game that followed in its footsteps.

A cultural touchstone for a generation, there are references to it littered throughout its gaming descendants and beyond, but there will now be an entirely new generation of player preparing to embark upon this chapter of the Zelda story - a good chunk of whom will have only experienced a Zelda title post-N64 (or no Zelda at all).

Which begs the question: will all those many, many references finally fall into place for them, like a well-constructed block-pushing puzzle?

It would be impossible to track it across all of gaming, of course, so instead we have listed some of our favourite and most obscure callbacks to the Ocarina of Time in the mainline Zelda games that came after. Grab a fresh cup of Lon Lon Milk for the read - there are a lot of them…

A bit of a false start, this, as essentially the entire game is a reference, utilising many of the same assets as its predecessor. But the story confirms Link isn’t the only person to make the trip from Hyrule to Termina - the game’s antagonist, Skull Kid, and The Happy Mask Salesman both recognise Link and mention his previous exploits.

Anju’s Grandmother is Granny in OoT, a different character who runs the potion shop and strokes a tiger cub in Hyrule. The tiger doesn’t make the jump to Termina, but there is a tiger portrait adorning the back of her wheelchair.

The 3DS adds a few more details. In the fishing hole, you can catch Lord Chapu-Chapu, a reference to OoT's giant fish/dungeon using a miniaturised version of its character model. And Ganondorf may be absent, but you can find a stuffed plushie of his horse on the floor in Romani’s Ranch.

After OoT released and canonically established itself as the Sealing War referenced in A Link to the Past’s manual, the opening text was changed in the GBA re-release from ‘seven wise men’ to ‘seven sages’ to directly reference the sages encountered in Ocarina of Time. Neat!

Wind Waker is positively awash with references, so let’s tackle some obscure ones.

A lot of musical themes, phrases and variations are used, and though Outset Island, where Link starts his adventure, has its own theme, it features a phrase lifted straight out of Kokiri Forest.

The Water Spirit Jabun’s theme is a callback to the theme inside Lord Jabu-Jabu (minus his tummy grumbles); however, a cheeky nod to the Great Deku Tree lies within the Sacred Shrines dotted around the great sea. The theme inside these is a variation on Link’s first OoT dungeon.

Speaking of smaller islands, the Goddess Statues on the Triangle Islands bear inscriptions on their bases which translate to Din’s Fire, Nauru’s Love, and Farore’s Wind - the spells Link can summon in OoT.

Ganondorf and the Great Deku Tree are canonically the same characters (the latter having grown from his sprout), but perhaps the most wild callback is a Rito named Koboli. The Nintendo Gallery within Wind Waker states that he is descended from three generations of Postmen and had an ancestor who was one. Take a close look and you can see that his face is modelled after the postman in Majora's Mask, who is of course the running man in OoT.

The Nintendo Gallery houses some more of our favourite easter eggs. There are bottles of Lon Lon Milk as well as the Bunny Hood and Keaton Mask up on the wall, but just behind the desk to the left is an unfinished bust of a character - the face shape and hairstyle clearly indicate this is a bust of the Kokiri sage, Saria.

That’s far from the only nod to the sages. The Master Sword chamber’s stained glass windows are pretty well known, but Wind Waker’s Kokiri sage Fado is also named after the girl who sits above the shop in Kokiri Forest. His role as the Sage of Wind is another nod to OoT, as the Forest Temple was originally intended to be the Wind Temple, something you can still see in the game by the medallion featuring a fan blade pattern.

The other sage, Medli, is a descendant of the Zora. Like Ruto was to Lord Jabu-Jabu, Medli is the attendant to the Rito's deity, Valoo, and the dungeon has Link haul Medli around above his head, just as you did with Princess Ruto.

To finish on a fun one, Wind Waker once again gives Link the ability to use a glass bottle to deflect Phantom Ganon’s energy balls back at him during Dead Man’s Volley, just like you could in OoT!

There seems to be a pattern of the top-down 2D games paying greater tribute to A Link to the Past. Nevertheless, Minish Cap does feature a few OoT nods.

There are a couple of audio callbacks that are really tricky to catch - the Kokiri Forest theme is remixed here to form the Hyrule Town music, while Link’s voice also samples child Link from OoT.

Popular characters return. As does Dampé. And there are some carpenters and builders in Minish Cap that share the design aesthetic from the carpenters on the N64.

A nice thematic nod is the set-piece routine of rescuing Princess Zelda after battling Vaati, only to have to escort her out as the castle crumbles down around you both. Subtle, but undeniable.

The obvious one here is that the overworld map very closely resembles the Ocarina's Hyrule. The Forest, Death Mountain, Lake Hylia, and Gerudo Desert all return and are more or less where you’d expect them to be, though you may not have caught this if, like so many of us, you played Twilight Princess on the Wii first (it mirrored the game world so East became West).

Three of the game’s Light Spirits — Eldin, Lanayru, and Faron — are named after the Hylian Goddesses, who themselves are depicted in a carving above Zelda’s throne portraying the creation myth from OoT's cutscene.

Ganondorf is, yet again, the same Ganondorf you fought in OoT and there’s a few other cool character nods, too. Skull Kid in the Lost Woods is accompanied by Saria’s Song, the same piece you taught Skull Kid in OoT, and Majora’s Mask antagonist. A popular fan theory is that he returned to Hyrule and, possibly being an immortal creature, agreed to guard the Master Sword for his good friend who helped him in Termina.

The fishing hole in Hyrule is run by Hena, the descendant of the owner of the fishing hole in OoT, of whom there is a black-and-white portrait behind the desk. She even has the same itchy back affliction shared by her forefather.

The White Wolf/Heroes Shade is the deceased, spectral reincarnation of the Hero of Time from OoT, which explains why the Howling Stones it gets you to use feature both the Prelude of Light and the Requiem of Spirit.

These are many more musical references, including the Serenade of Water playing whenever you talk to Rutella, Queen of the Zora, but she and her son, Prince Ralis, also sport necklaces featuring a pendant that resembles the Zora Sapphire.

Oh, and we can once again enjoy a game of Dead Man’s Volley with an empty bottle. Huzzah!

Where Wind Waker was stuffed with OoT callbacks, its DS sequels are substantially less so. However, a fairy companion returns for this game and shares the same design as Navi. Gossip Stones made an appearance, too.

The A Spirit Opens the Way track is a variation of the Creation of Hyrule theme from OoT - not one that’s sampled often. I also maintain that Spirit Tracks' Dungeon Gauntlet theme is a remix of the Battle theme that plays during the fight with Gohma, but someone with a better ear might disagree.

Being a game that launched on the 25th anniversary of the Zelda series, Skyward Sword has some choice OoT nods.

Just like the DS pair of games, the Gossip Stones are back, but this time they share a secret with OoT: flinging a bomb at one will cause it to count down and launch into the air like a rocket.

Loftwings, the bird companions of the game, are a callback/forward to OoT’s iconic Hylian Shield - in particular Link’s red Loftwing, which matches the hue of the bird on the shield’s front.

A strong visual nod occurs once the Isle of the Goddess falls into the Sealed Grounds. Looking up into the ceiling of the newly formed Sealed Temple reveals a mural of the Triforce surrounded by the sage medallions, which in itself bears a striking resemblance to the Chamber of Sages Link returns to after clearing a temple.

In this game, Zelda hands over a precious, magical instrument to Link before her own power awakens later on in the game, just like Zelda in OoT.

Lastly, a puzzle and thematic callback. The Lanayru Mining Facility contains a puzzle where you have to hit three switches in a specific order — 2, 3, 1 — a reference to the final puzzle of OoT’s Great Deku Tree. “23 is number 1!”

A few characters pop up here, with Dampé appearing again, not once, but twice. He’s his own parallel in both Hyrule and Lorule.

Hyrule’s unnamed Milk Bar owner also bears a striking resemblance to Talon, while his Lorule counterpart looks suspiciously like Ingo.

Two pieces of art reference OoT: a painting of a fairy design like Navi’s adorning the wall of the Stylish Woman’s House, while a small, yellowish Ocarina is on Link's wall. Easy to miss, as you need to merge into the wall to find them.

If you dash into a wall within the level lobby, there’s a chance it will drop a purple ball down. Give it a whack with your sword and you have a chance of hearing the Lost Woods theme, Zelda’s Lullaby, the Lon Lon Ranch theme or Kakariko’s Windmill theme. They only play while you juggle the ball with sword hits - once it hits the floor, it’s done!

My favourite, though, is that Link is assigned voice clips from one of four Zelda games when you create a save file. So there’s a 25% chance you’ll be hearing the guttural shouts of OoT Link while you play.

Breath of the Wild's vast map is heaving with references to other Zelda games. There’s some obvious callbacks like Ruto Lake, Mido Swamp, and Mount Nabooru, but perhaps the best callback is Koukot Plateau by the Gerudo Desert - named, fittingly, as a portmanteau of Kotake and Koume.

Eldin, Faron, and Lanayru have been used in reference to the Goddesses before, but the dragons Dinraal, Farosh, and Naydra are also named after OoT’s deities.

The Temple of Time on the Great Plateau is the classic structure from OoT, even playing the same theme inside, but a sneakier callback lies within the Ranch Ruins just south of Hyrule Castle, which perfectly mirrors the race track and layout of Lon Lon Ranch.

Some of the clothing and weapons in the game, particularly the DLC sets, straight up lift costumes from OoT, but a sneakier nod is the design of the Forest Dweller's Sword, based on the Kokiri Sword, and is even clearer to see in the upcoming remake.

And my favourite costume nod doesn’t belong to Link. Hudson, a man who builds houses from the ground up, is modelled on the carpenters in OoT.

There’s plenty of musical references, too, including one you can see but not hear. Above the throne in Hyrule Castle, there’s a Triforce surrounded by concentric rings with round dots placed along them. On closer inspection, these rings actually form a musical stave, with the dots being the notes for Zelda’s Lullaby that you learned in OoT. Incredible nod.

An incredibly faithful remake of the Game Boy original that predates OoT, the Switch version nevertheless manages to add a few nods.

Dampé is back. At this point it feels like he’s in more games than Link?

When fighting Shadow Nightmare, the ability to play Dead Man’s Volley with Agahnim’s Shadow has been retroactively added, too.

Building on the incredible reference work of BOTW, Link can now hum any of the following while cooking: Saria’s Song, Epona’s Song, or the Song of Storms, while the House theme returns for Link’s home.

The flute player Pyper raises his legs to the side in turn as he plays, a direct callback to the flute-playing skull kids in the Lost Woods.

Cutscenes deliberately evoke previous OoT ones here. Zelda’s turn and gasp in the opening, with her right hand to her mouth, is an homage to her seeing Link for the first time in OoT, while the memory A Show of Fealty mirrors what Zelda sees through the window in that very same scene - Ganondorf kneeling before the King while swearing a false oath.

Though not named, Ganondorf is also flanked by Kotake and Koume in the above and other scenes, distinguishable by the gems on their forehead and the cloths on their shoulder matching their OoT headbands.

Some conceptual nods include Ganondorf being imprisoned and sealed by seven sages, while the adventure sees Hyrule Castle raised up high above a red, ominous pit, just as it is once Link travels into the future in Ocarina of Time.

Echoes of Wisdom’s opening cutscene deliberately evokes the climax of OoT (which itself evoked past games) before switching things up, with Zelda trapped in a purple crystal and held aloft, but the whole game also heavily references the creation of myth from OoT while expanding upon it.

Kakariko Village, although appearing in several 2D Zelda games, specifically features a windmill, a graveyard, and a well (although it is covered) for the first time since OoT.

So that’s it: our favourite and most obscure Ocarina of Time nods, references, and easter eggs across the Zelda series.

There are many others, of course, and in other games. The Oracle duo, for instance, are packed with characters from Ocarina of Time - most notably giving human form to the Golden Goddesses for the first time, while also fleshing out Kotake and Koume. Elsewhere, Kaepora Gaebora, Malon and Talon, and Dampé (of all people) returned in Four Swords Adventures. As did Epona! Curiously also split into four, somehow.

There are so many references that this article was literally double the word count on draft one! But which reference is your favourite? Is there another we should’ve included? If so, give us a ‘Hey, Listen!’ in the comments below.

And before we go, a big shoutout to Zeltik, DPadGamer, A Dan in Time, Triforce Times, DidYouKnowGaming, Zelda Dungeon, Zelda Wiki, and Kevin Armes Music for their incredible work cataloguing Easter Eggs across the Zelda series.

George is a stage and screen actor and voiceover artist with a deep love of gaming and all things Nintendo. His writing has appeared on Nintendo Life and Time Extension, and he's the host of NintenDormant.

#4148. Captivating cosmic megastructure adventure game Hypnos leaves early access next week, offering up a world I'm desperate to dig into further

Do I know what's going on in it yet? Well...

I just love me a megastructure, I do. I'm not entirely sure why, to be honest. My best guess is that growing up in a major city with concrete pillars looming over me higher into the sky than I care to take notice of, perhaps even threatening me, left me with a sense of awe towards that which exists at a scale I can't really comprehend. With that, I was quite quickly hooked on whatever Hypnos was putting down, even if when I first had a go at it I couldn't quite tell you what was going on. And now, after a stint in early access, the eldritch "megastructure fever dream," is launching into 1.0 in just a week's time!

To be specific, that's October 29th, just a couple of days shy of good ole Hallow's Eve, which given the unearthly vibes of Hypnos definitely feels somewhat appropriate. For those not yet ingratiated into the sights and wonders of Hypnos, it is a first-person adventure and exploration game; more than the humble walking simulator, though perhaps not as involved as puzzle games with similar vibes. You won't just be walking, but chatting to folks, all manner of strange inhabitants, often speaking in cryptic ways.

The character you play as is an equally sickly-looking and handsome hot boy named Chrono, who wants to find "the faceless boy," i.e. Matthew. As Chrono, you are tasked with solving "city's mysteries, face the Monarchs who rule the far reaches of the world and cross the veils that separate ignorance from truth." A tall order! But a vibey one, and those chats you'll be having are certainly visual novel like in that there are multiple dialogue choices you can make that can lead to different endings.

I haven't had time to dig into Hypnos as much as I would have liked since it arrived in early access, but now that it is launching into 1.0, I suppose I don't really have all that much of a choice! And if you're curious about it yourself, you can just pick it up right now in early access (the price is staying the same), or have a go at the demo on Steam if you need some extra convincing.

#4147. Naval warfare, an actual server browser and more on the way to Battlefield 6 this year as BF Studios reveals 2026 roadmap

2026 is looking very exciting for Battlefield 6, even if much of what's coming is based on things we already know, and some we've long been asking for.

It took Battlefield Studios over four months to tell Battlefield 6 players what they can actually expect from the game over the course of this year, in terms of content - but we’re glad to see a plan laid out nonetheless.

The developer unveiled a grand 2026 roadmap, covering three more seasons currently in the works, and a wealth of new additions across the entire game, including new maps and the introduction of a new theatre of combat.

In a wide-ranging new video dubbed The Year Ahead, members of the Battlefield 6 development team have revealed a lot of new information about the future of the multiplayer shooter, going over plenty of the features and new content coming over the course of this year.

The video confirmed that BF6 has at least three other seasons in the works. Season 3, which begins in May, will be followed by Season 4, and Season 5 later in the year. Season 5 is the most mysterious, which is understandable.

We’ve known about some of what’s coming in Season 3, such as the remake of Golmud Railway (now called Railway to Golmud), but the video also revealed that a remake of Battlefield 3’s Grand Bazaar - now Cairo Bazaar - will also arrive later in the same season. Other exciting additions, such as battle royale solos and ranked play for Redsec are also on the agenda for Season 3.

Season 4, set for July, looks to be the biggest so far, with the introduction of naval combat, which will be available across two maps. Tsuru Reef, which is said to be even larger than Golmud, the largest map in BF6. The Pacific-set map won’t be the only one, as later in the season, another remake will arrive, this time of the iconic Wake Island.

The introduction of naval combat will bring with it a new dynamic wave system, aircraft carriers with operational flight decks, and new naval vehicles. Custom lobbies and Spectator Mode are also planned for Season 4.

Season 5 will bring three maps to BF6, rather than two, but all of its content remains under wraps.

Perhaps a sour note is that almost all of the maps referenced and shown in the video are remakes of maps from other Battlefield games, or reimagined at the very least. The Battlefield series is no stranger to remaking its own maps, but Battlefield 6 appears to be leaning on it much more than past entries.

If it’s any consolation, however, the map remakes we’ve played so far in Battlefield 6 have gone through major changes that have contributed to giving them a different flow and feel from their classic versions, or even remakes in other BF games.

Over the course of 2026, you can also expect the return of persistent servers, as well as a server browser to find them all - just like the good ol’ days. This includes the ability to host your own, though it’s unclear quite how this is going to work.

Season 3 is set to revealed in the coming days, so you’ll be hearing back from BF Studios in the near future.

#4146. Poll: So, How Many Xbox Mythic Achievements Do You Have So Far?

Xbox's Platinum Trophy equivalent was made public earlier this week, and it's been exciting to see just how many Mythic Achievements we've unlocked since we first picked up an Xbox 360 controller.

Mythic Achievements are an additional reward for unlocking all of a game's base achievements to reach 100% completion. As it stands, Pure Xbox Editor Fraser Gilbert is rocking 8 Mythics, with the likes of FIFA 14, Rocket League, and a bunch of Telltale's The Walking Dead games. Whereas, Staff Writer Craig Reid picked up 36 Mythics playing titles such as Alan Wake II, Signalis, End of Abyss, and the wonderful, Duck Detective: The Ghost of Glamping.

Craig is currently toying with the idea of starting a new "Become Mythic" feature. The idea is to post an article for every Mythic earned, describing what it was like to unlock the achievement, talk about the game a little bit, and to see how many he can get in a year. It's not an original concept - in fact, it's inspired by our sister site Push Square's 'Going Platinum' feature written by the lovely Stephen Tailby.

We think these new full-completion accolades are a very smart addition to the Xbox console experience, and we'd really like to know just how many our lovely Pure Xbox community has.

So, let's hear it, gang! Tell us how many Mythic Achievements you have by voting in the poll below, as well as sharing your most favourite Mythic'd game in the comments section.

#4145. PS5 Adds Another Free Open World Game to Your Rotation with Surprise Silver Palace Release Date

Victorian-inspired free-to-play open world game Silver Palace will release worldwide on 14th December, which has really shocked me.

I played this stylish effort at Gamescom earlier in the year, but assumed it was still quite a way away.

But in a shock reveal overnight, publisher Elementa has confirmed the title will deploy on the PS5 in just a few short weeks.

Pre-registration is available now across all platforms, with various milestones, including a free 4-Star character. The first target has already been achieved, and you can follow the progress through here.

I assume PS Store wishlisting contributes to the pre-registration targets, and you can do that through here.

Silver Palace is very much a gacha game in the same style as Genshin Impact, although I think its regal sandbox gives it a slightly different flavour to anything else on the market.

In its official blurb, Elementa describes it as a game “centred around detective mysteries”. Some of the production values in the Gamescom demo I played blew me away.

There’s also a new trailer which introduces the character Gratia. I think the voice work is fun, and this trailer had a lot more personality than past ones – although I do think, at its core, this title is treading familiar ground.

I don’t really have enough time in my life for another gacha game, but I’ll be sure to give this one a try over Christmas and bring you a review. I assume we’ll get lots more information in the weeks leading up to launch as well.

#4144. Diablo 4's next season won't have any new mechanics or a new theme because all the focus is on Lord of Hatred

If you don't intend to buy the Lord of Hatred expansion, the next season in Diablo 4 won't be as exciting as you'd expect.

Diablo 4 is gearing up for its biggest post-launch event yet: the upcoming release of the Lord of Hatred expansion. As was the case with Vessel of Hatred before it, expansion releases alter the seasonal flow in a few ways, and Blizzard has now explained how.

The game’s next season - its 13th - has been officially revealed as Season of Reckoning. The new season will kick off alongside the expansion’s release next week, and will be available to all players, just like all previous seasons.

Although Season of Reckoning will roll out as normal, the season itself won’t be as meaty, at least when it comes to the sort of gameplay mechanics and themes players have come to expect from each new season.

You’ll still find the normal Season Rank chase, Smoldering Ashes, and various rewards at each chapter. Season Blessings will also return, but that’s about it for progression outside of the game itself. If it’s any consolation, there are more goals and objectives to tackle this season.

The even better news is that, according to Blizzard, future seasons will follow the classic format, which makes sense. The new season will come with a battle pass, of course, featuring four Reliquaries, as usual. The first Reliquary is free, while the others are paid.

Blizzard has also confirmed the the pre-load for Lord of Hatred is available now on all platforms. Even if you’re not getting the expansion, patch 3.0.0's pre-load includes all expansion content regardless, so you may as well pre-download it to be ready for April 27/28. On launch day, you’ll also need to download a smaller patch, version 3.0.1.

In case you missed it, we published our Lord of Hatred review earlier in the week. Give it a read if you’re curious about the expansion’s impact on the narrative, and how it changes core Diablo 4 gameplay.

#4143. Even at their most chaotic and conflicted, BioWare were the heart of the western computer RPG

Life... is strength. The gears of this world are tuned for a quick death. Doomity-doom-doom! We is all doooooo-oooomed! The Guardian says for me to be cheerful, and to not repeat what he says all the... oh. I'm Commander Shepard, and this is my favourite store on the Citadel. You simians may merely refer to me as 'Sir,' if you prefer a less... syllable-intensive workout. I have seen the throne of the Gods, and it was empty. Stand in the ashes of a trillion dead souls and ask the ghosts if honour matters. There are people like you everywhere. It's just that not everyone has the words for it yet. You exist because we allow it, and you will end because we demand it. Let's call that finished. You must gather your party before venturing forth.

I'm not even all that much of a BioWare enthusiast. I'm not sure I'm in mourning, exactly. Partly that's because videogame studios are big corporate abstractions, unworthy of our silly human emotions; the story here is that a bunch of people have lost their livelihoods, after their employers triumphantly thrust themselves into unbelievable debt. And partly it's because, as with any studio of over 30 years standing, BioWare was a much-caulked and jury-rigged ship of Theseus – paddling around in the doldrums of 2026, I'm not entirely sure what I should be mourning, any more.

Reportedly, there were around 50 staff left at BioWare, mostly labouring away on Mass Effect 5, when EA closed them this week. A lot of those who worked on the studio's formative games, including the very first Baldur's Gate, are long departed. The past decade especially has seen a steady exodus of BioWare talent, alongside a barrage of "veteran" start-ups and spiritual successor projects, many of which have sadly now faded and folded.

Within that arc, my own appreciation for BioWare has waxed and waned. I honestly can't remember enough of Baldur's Gate 2 to have strong opinions, though I overall acknowledge its brilliance. I probably felt closest to the studio during the heyday of the original Mass Effect trilogy. The original's Vigil scene still gives me shivers, and who could forget the prodigious act of fan service demolition that was Mass Effect 2's opening, to say nothing of its legendary "Suicide Mission" (I left Mordin behind).

I will always carry a candle for Dragon Age: Inquisition – a generous and unwieldy return to save-the-world-dom after Dragon Age 2's leaner city story, which I cherish for its beautiful Tarot art, its bustling hub castle, and its spread of rambunctious and difficult companion characters. I greatly enjoy Ferelden as a setting, all the different yarns the various races spin about the world's becoming. Still, I bounced right off Dragon Age: The Veilguard's on-the-nose, corridor-like design, despite Nic's guarded exhortations.

Anthem? I was keener on that than a lot of you, but I remember it mostly as a conflicted yet promising aviator with nowhere to go – so much BioWare flourish, floundering through a swamp of live service. I thought Mass Effect: Andromeda was a wide, shallow bowl of lukewarm space-gruel lent relish only by its launch bugs. There are other BioWare games I simply haven't played – Neverwinter Nights (well, apart from the five minutes I managed, before it became clear my computer at the time really couldn't run it) and its celebrated modding toolkit, the Orientalised fable Jade Empire and, whisper it, almighty KOTOR.

As for my experience of BioWare as a games journalist, it's pretty brief and polarised. On the one hand, spending three hours with a preview build of Inquisition in a London warehouse, alongside such guiding lights as former PCGamer scribe Chris Thursten, is probably as close to heaven as I'll get before my inevitable deathbed recantation. On the other, there was that humiliating interview with co-founder Dr Ray Muzyka, when I was terrified our mic wouldn't record him properly. I resorted to kneeling between Muzyka and the actual interviewer, jerking the dictaphone back and forth in my desperation to guzzle up every last drop of Muzyka wisdom. Not even Khalisah al-Jilani was this cringe. I haven't been allowed near a BioWare executive since.

The thing is, you don't have to have enjoyed, or even played many BioWare games to understand the difference they've made, and why the newly private EA's closure of the studio is such a kick in the guts, however presaged by years of interference, mismanagement, and neglect. As regards North American and European sci-fantasy incarnations, at least, BioWare have always been the RPG's sleeping sentinel. They wrote the genre around themselves, producing and revising a vocabulary over decades that so many other designers, writers and modders are in conversation with – whether courting comparison, or critiquing and even despising.

BioWare are why D&D RPGs took off. They're the creators of by far the most influential adaptation of the tabletop game's forbidding ruleset. They are the studio you probably think of, when you think of party-based stories with branching plots. They are the blockbuster joint you think of, rivalled only by Final Fantasy and more recently Larian, when you think of companions who deserve the starring role.

Even their stumbles have thrown open ground for other writers, designers and artists to investigate: that main-and-supporting-band antagonism between critical path and sidequest, for example - between yet another chronicle of destined heroes averting some great evil, and the huggable humour of playing go-between for a knight who's too shy to hit on somebody. How to reconcile the grandiosity with the closeness is the trad fantasy RPG's founding dilemma. They popularised in-game romances and, yes, sex scenes that generally feel like the convincing result of hours of careful narrative distillation, and occasionally like a helping of cheesecake unlocked by pawing away at a hidden skilltree.

They are the studio who got us tallying up colour-coded Good and Bad points to shape both protagonist and endgame - so tacky, but undeniably striking as a vehicle for stark shifts and flavourful writing, as demonstrated in reverse by the omnivorous wishy-washiness of Mass Effect: Andromeda. Their morality systems are a place from which to start thinking about other, less videogamey, more organic and conflicting entanglements of Morality and System. They introduced a particular species of videogame celebrity with Commander Shepard, and they presided over a very particular stage in the evolving friction between creators and "audience" with Mass Effect 3's much-revised ending. While I'd made up my mind to stop covering EA games, following the Saudi-led acquisition, I was curious, if not optimistic, to see what they might have done with Mass Effect 5.

Above all, BioWare were the wizards of words. They had less-good scripts but I don't think they ever penned a bad one. Looking back over their games is dizzying and deafening, like opening a door in a dark, crumbling house to reveal a crowd of revellers - demons and courtesans and krogans and fops and berserkers, painted glorious shades by secret firelight and dancing in a ring.

So many words! How many words? Tens of millions, surely. Words that conjure words, raising them from the dust: Go for the optics, Chatika! Go for the eyes, Boo! Words seemingly drawn from some personal well of pain and tenderness, easily reduced to authorial self-commentary, that stick in my mind where so much else about the ageing fantasy has lost its charm. Here is Aveline, the aforesaid timid knight, to play us out. "That big man made every step of the story my choice. I loved that. He died of the Wasting in a Denerim ward... those last weeks, I read to him. I had to take his hand to turn the pages, and I couldn't tell if he was too weak, or if it was the old game. He smiled at that, his big girl… Don't let anyone tell you how to mourn. And when someone says 'move on', you take their hand and say, 'my choice.'"
