#4116. Arkane survival negotiations reportedly seeing "several forms of takeover" considered ahead of November deadline, as Marvel's Blade production nears end

217 jobs are on the line at the studio, report claims

Update: A Microsoft rep has told PC Gamer that the company have "extended the consultation period by one additional month as we explore options, including finding a partner to support [Arkane] through the development work still ahead." "This is a defined extension," they added, "and we remain committed to keeping the Works Council informed throughout the process."

So, Microsoft's consultation with Arkane's Social and Economic Committee now looks set to roll on until December 13th. Though, as we previously noted, the Printemps Écologique union have said that this consultation deadline isn't the deadline by which Arkane need to have found a buyer, with the setting of the latter deadline being one of the things that needs to take place as part of the ongoing negotiations.

Negotiations over the future of Dishonored and Deathloop developers Arkane Lyon are reportedly seeing "several forms of takeover" considered as a November deadline looms for the divorce Xbox set in motion back in July. French law makes the process of shuttering or chucking away studios a lot harder for companies like Microsoft than it is elsewhere in the world, hence Arkane's fate still being up in the air while production work on Marvel's Blade nears completion according to the report.

French publication Le Monde are behind this paywalled report on how the negotiations between the two sides are going. They note that due to a French law brought in as of 2014, companies with more than 1000 staff have to search for a buyer for three months before they can throw up their hands and shut up shop. In the case of Arkane Lyon, the report says 217 jobs are at risk.

The deadline for these consultations with Arkane's Social and Economic Committee (via Gematsu) is November 13th, though Arkane have longer than that to pin down a buyer for the studio - speaking to RPS, a Printemps Écologique union representative clarified that the exact date is being negotiated and subject to change.

The Le Monde report also cites a representative of Printemps Écologique, who along with the Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Video (STJV) union seemingly aren't too happy with Microsoft's attitude throughout the process so far.

Microsoft have told Le Monde that they're "actively seeking a partner to support the next phase of development and enable the commercialisation of the [Marvel’s Blade] project". According to a union rep cited in the report, the superhero game is "nearing the end" of production, with the unions understandably backing Arkane's work and hoping that it will see the light of day.

Xbox wrote as part of an announcement of layoffs in September - the second of multiple waves in a mass chopping that still isn't over as of writing - that they expected consultation over how Arkane will move forward "to continue through the end of the year".

Solidarity to all of the developers at Arkane and here's hoping these negotiations do end with a result that keeps the maximum amount of them in work and making the games they want to make.

This article has been updated to clarify that the deadline for Arkane finding a buyer isn't the same as the deadline for the consultation period.

#4114. HoYoverse's Animal Crossing Rival Skips PS5 for Switch 2

HoYoverse is undoubtedly gunning for the Animal Crossing audience with its next title Petit Planet, so it’s perhaps no surprise to see the Chinese dev focus on Switch 2 with its upcoming cosy title.

However, it’s noteworthy as the juggernaut Chinese dev has brought practically all of its releases to Sony’s system since Genshin Impact – the ginormous open world RPG which launched during the peak of the pandemic in 2020.

It’s worth noting that HoYoverse had intended to bring Genshin Impact to the original Switch years ago, but this port famously never materialised.

Petit Planet will launch on 4th December for PC and mobile, but during a Special Programme earlier today, the dev committed to a Switch 2 release in 2027. It didn’t mention any other consoles, like the PS5.

Given that HoYoverse already has a massive PlayStation fanbase, its social media accounts are already being targeted with queries about a PS5 version. I wouldn’t be surprised if it does end up on Sony’s console eventually.

I do think Switch 2 makes sense for this particular title, as it’s clear the dev is trying to peel players away from Animal Crossing. I also can see how the cosy game format works best on mobile formats.

But considering Tom Nook and co will likely return on Nintendo’s console at some point in the future, I do wonder whether there might be an opportunity bringing this game to the PS5, where the only other competitor I can think of is Disney Dreamlight Valley and maybe Infinity Nikki.

I’ll ask HoYoverse whether it has any plans to release Petit Planet on other platforms in the future.

In the meantime, you can get a taste of the title in the Special Programme embedded above, and also pre-register for various rewards on the game’s official website if you’re interested.

#4113. Woim is the earth-guzzling, self-bisecting sokoban pick-me-up I needed after a week of games industry disasters

While ladling city-builders into the Maw's feeding trough this week, I remarked that being a worm must really suck. Then came the closure of BioWare, layoffs across other EA studios, further depressing genAI revelations, allegations of antisemitism at indie gaming events, a big Capcom data breach, and yet more worrying tidyings about Arkane.

I rescind my earlier observation: I would like to be a worm. A happy little worm, tunnelling after golden apples in the moist and forgiving earth, where there are no emails or press releases at all. The only thing I have to worry about down here is my butt growing so big I get stuck behind it. And also getting chopped in half by sliding doors, but it turns out this may actually help with the first problem. See for yourself - video below.

Ah, to be a soil-dwelling invertebrate in Woim, a puzzle game with a touch of the sokobans, consisting of 50 levels and an unspecified quantity of secrets, scattered across four subterranean worlds. The idea in each level is to crawl around a grid layout to reach a golden apple, opening the exit.

As with non-videogame worms, this involves a certain amount of ingesting earth and pooping it out behind you, but you can't just devour the whole layout. You'll need to guzzle red apples that make you longer, so that you can (for example) keep pressing a switch with your body as you slither towards a door. Or you might have to shove a rock onto that switch. Or shove that rock onto a water jet to propel it somewhere you can't reach.

Later on, there are breakable eggs that must be carried to nests, daisies that push back outward when you take your weight off them, scissors with which to snip yourself into separately functioning halves, and hats. I don't think this is an entirely accurate worm simulator. As in sokoban, the major problem is trapping yourself, but you can undo moves without penalty by tapping Z.

I've played six levels, and it's a jolly production. The music wobbles and boobles along, and your worm has a habit of looking at you expectantly when you get stuck that makes me giggle. Read more about it on Steam. If, unlike me, you've had a really uplifting week and are in sore need of a sokobanlike charged with maximum ontological dread, may I recommend Void Stranger.

#4111. Former Xbox Manager Explains Why $500M Cost For Gears: E-Day Doesn't Tell The Whole Story

Update [Mon 2nd Nov 2026, 1pm]: Windows Central's Jez Corden has weighed in with a few extra details this morning as well, explaining that according to a "variety of trusted sources", The Coalition has been contributing to many other Xbox projects over the past 6-7 years.

All of these seemingly factor into the $500M budget that has been attributed, although it's unknown to what extent.

"...The Coalition worked for over a year and a half on a prototype project for Xbox that Windows Central understands was ultimately canceled. The Coalition also worked on Avowed, Hellblade 2, Clockwork Revolution, State of Decay 3, Grounded and Grounded 2, and has even contributed to the upcoming StarCraft reboot."

"The Coalition also spent a great deal of time working with Epic Games on the "Matrix Awakens" Unreal Engine demonstration, as well as the Alpha Point demo, both of which were intended to showcase the potential of UE5 on next-gen consoles and PCs."

Nevertheless, Corden warns that $500 million is a "lot of money to invest without a specific structure in place to explain why some of these costs were worthwhile to Microsoft auditors", and that there have even been "some internal disagreements over how exactly attribution should be distributed".

Original Story: Over the past couple of weeks, there's been a lot of chatter about a rumoured $500 million cost for The Coalition to make Gears of War: E-Day, alongside debates about how much of that money went on the game itself.

Speaking on the weekend, former Xbox exec Derek Reese shared his take on the situation, suggesting that The Coalition is heavily involved with supporting Microsoft's branch of the Unreal Engine, which is where a lot of the cost goes.

Here's what the ex-Senior Product Manager of Xbox Game Services had to say:

So much of that cost is The Coalition being on the hook for the Microsoft branch of Unreal and one of the flagship titles. I should know, I tried to get leadership to support a plan to have other studios adopt it and write off the support costs. Same problem with Turn10 and ForzaTech.

This aligns with what Jez Corden of Windows Central was saying a few weeks ago as well, who originally suggested that because The Coalition is "the technological glue for all of Xbox", some of that money is "spread across the entire portfolio" and even goes towards The Coalition's help on other Xbox games like Fable and Forza Horizon.

Corden confirmed yesterday that Reese's comments align with what he's heard:

In some follow-up posts, Reese mentioned that he thinks The Coalition "accomplished their end goals very well and delivered a great accomplishment in E-Day", while also suggesting that there's a "publicly visible pattern of allowing departments to shoulder the costs of leadership direction", pointing to Double Fine as a recent notable example.

So, hopefully we can put this one to bed now! It seems the $500 million budget IS a legit figure for Gears of War: E-Day, but it's hard to realistically attribute that entire figure to the game itself.

The big question is what Xbox thinks about all of this, including whether the game has been a success in terms of sales, Premium Upgrade conversions, Xbox Game Pass subscriptions and its pulling power as an Xbox console exclusive, and it could be some time until we know the answer to that.

News Rumours Persist That Xbox Spent $500 Million On Gears Of War: E-Day, Despite Some Objections

Review Gears Of War: E-Day (Campaign) - A Monumental Triumph For Xbox, And My Game Of The Year

E-Day exceeded expectations and made me fall in love with the series even more

Fraser is the News Editor at Pure Xbox, where he spends his time reporting on the biggest stories in the world of Xbox and beyond.

ANY well managed corporation has a time management system where employees and contractors register their time and what project they were working on. Even if they are salaried employees that don’t get paid by the hour. This is used not only to track personal time off and/or sick time but also precisely to manage independent project budgets.

It can sometimes be annoying as an employee that works full time in a single project (as those employees might see it as pointless), but it’s vital for management to know what projects (not teams) are eating up money.

However, someone somewhere in a position of leadership at Xbox should know what the game did cost to make, and you'd think they would be quick to refute the $500 million rumour and counter it with a more precise figure.

I have said often now that I think the budget on display is far more likely to fall somewhere between $200 million and $300 million. The game oozes quality, and that will not have come cheap.

I'd also like to see addressed the (frankly ridiculous) rumour that a further $500 million spent on publicity for the game. If it is true that the original rumour (of $500 million) did not include publicity, then that does mean more still will have been spent on it (although I do not believe the $500 million rumour that was circulating last week).

The one thing I would say is that even if the budget is a 'low' as $200 million (including publicity), there is no way the game managed to recoup very much of it at all, and it does lead me to fear both for the future of The Coalition and for the Gears of War Franchise. I foresee Sharma taking a chainsaw to The Coalition in March or April next year, and it's not going to be pretty...

#4110. "This was not a Creative Assembly developed game": Total War boss points the finger at external partner for Shogun 2 Complete Edition disaster

But concedes that "we took our eyes off" its creation

Last week, Creative Assembly and Sega pulled Total War: Shogun 2's remastered Complete Edition from Steam, after an avalanche of complaints about technical problems and some AI-generated art. Now, Total War vice president Roger Collum has written a personal apology, while pinning some of the blame on an unnamed external partner. He's also clarified Creative Assembly's stance on generative AI, conceding that the studio do use it to help with "analysis, debugging, or speedy prototyping", but that they're against using it to generate game assets and art.

"I get many of you are angry and disappointed about the state of the Shogun 2: Complete Edition release," Collum writes on the official Twar Reddit. "We are too – especially the team members who have put everything into Total War games for years, some even decades. This was not a Creative Assembly developed game. It wasn’t subject to our same internal reviews and quality assurance. We took our eyes off its external development, with all our teams focused on our next big projects. However, whatever the development arrangements, Total War is our franchise and our name is on it."

Again, Collum doesn't name the external developer in question, but Mataboo Games are listed as co-devs on the Steam page. Collum says that SEGA and a small team of senior developers are working with the external team on "next steps", with details to follow. In the meantime, he has some general thoughts on how and when the Twarfolk make use of generative AI tools.

"I want to be very clear on the studio-wide stance on generative AI, because I know there are many questions about where we stand," Collum writes. "We are a craft studio. Our games are made by incredibly talented people, and we do not believe in a world where technology replaces the creativity of humans. At Creative Assembly we do not use generative AI to create game assets, including AI-generated art. We demand the same of any external developers we work with. The situation with Shogun 2: Complete Edition is being investigated."

Collum adds that Creative Assembly do, however, use AI tools for "support" purposes. "It shouldn’t replace the creator," he says. "I don’t believe that AI can replace the human experience, judgement and creativity that awesome experiences come from. Can AI tools help with analysis, debugging, or speedy prototyping so our experts can focus on making incredible games? Absolutely."

Collum ends his message by requesting that people don't abuse individual Total War developers. "Our community teams, QA, designers, and everyone in between are doing their job, as asked by the company," Collum writes. "Their safety is our priority. They do not deserve, and we will not tolerate, harassment or being singled out online and personally criticised." Collum warns that if you're nasty to developers, the studio may need to be less transparent in future.

I'm not sure I wholly buy the argument about "taking our eyes off" the game, given that Creative Assembly and Sega ran a bunch of trailers and marketing for it and sent round a FAQ detailing, among other things, how it would affect mods. While unavailable for purchase, the Complete Edition's Steam page is still live as of writing with "overwhelmingly negative" reviews. Creative Assembly and Sega have reinstated the original game's Steam page while they work on kicking the CE into shape.

#4109. The Rings of Power season 3 showrunner says the five-year jump takes us right to "the tipping point" of the "epic war"

Join the GamesRadar community for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Get the biggest gaming news, reviews, and releases straight to your inbox.

Bringing all the latest movie news, features, and reviews to your inbox

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Co-showrunner Patrick McKay says The Rings of Power season 3's five-year time jump allowed "the world to change"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's only been two real years since The Lord of the Rings prequel was on our screens, but five years will have passed when The Rings of Power season 3 picks up. However, showrunner Patrick McKay says the break has allowed Middle-earth to reach the point where war is brewing again, so we can dive right back into the action.

"The five-year jump allowed the story to have scope, for the world to change,” said co‑showrunner Patrick McKay in an interview with SFX Magazine. "The war has been raging across Middle-earth, and now we’re at a tipping point. Sauron has conquered everything except for two pockets of Elven resistance that are defended by their rings."

McKay continued, "This third season is where every single storyline becomes part of the large, epic war between Sauron and the Elves, and hopefully the show is deeper in its emotionality and the psychology of the characters."

Season 2 ended with the Dark Lord on top after killing Celebrimbor and securing the Nine Rings of Men. The Elves took another hit when Eregion fell under seige, leading the surviving Elves to flee to what will become known as Rivendell. Elsewhere, the Stranger was finally revealed as Gandalf, and Balrog was freed. From that point on, all sides have been preparing for war, as season 3 promises a fiery battle. Perhaps this is why McKay told SFX that The Rings of Power "hits its stride" in season 3.

According to the official synopsis from Amazon, we know that in the time that has passed, Sauron’s armies have started their march toward our heroes, with just a few sites left standing. That includes Khazad-dûm, where the Dwarves are sealed deep in the mountains, and the elven realms of Lindon and Rivendell. Now, Sauron sits in his tower in Mordor, growing even more enraged with the desire for domination. The Elves, Dwarves, Free Men, and Wizards must come together to prevent him from forging The One Ring to Rule Them All.

Season 3 welcomes back Morfydd Clark as Galadriel, Charlie Vickers as Sauron, and Daniel Weyman as Gandalf, and adds Jamie Campbell Bower as Galadriel's long-lost love, Celeborn.

The Rings of Power season 3 hits Prime Video on November 11. For more, check out our guides on how to watch The Lord of the Rings movies and shows in order and the Lord of the Rings timeline.

#4108. After Cancelling Zelda Switch 2 Pre-Orders, Walmart Is Now Supposedly Sending Out $519 Gift Cards

Some customers also claim they've been able to "reorder" the system

Last week, Walmart reportedly cancelled Zelda Switch 2 pre-orders a day before the launch after it "oversold" the consoles.

In an update, the retailer is apparently giving out vouchers in response to the upset these cancellations have caused. As highlighted by Polygon, some customers are now supposedly being compensated with "$519 gift cards".

Here's the email response customers are now receiving from Walmart (confirmed by deal website CheapAssGamer.com):

We know you were looking forward to your preorder of Nintendo Switch 2 Legend of Zelda, and we sincerely apologize that we canceled your pre-order. This was our mistake.

To show our appreciation for you as a Walmart customer and help make up for the canceled order, we're sending you a Walmart eGift Card for $519.99. You'll receive this gift card via email within 10 business days.

Again, we're sorry for the mistake. Thank you for being a Walmart customer. We look forward to serving you again soon.

According to the same story, these customers are also being given the chance to reorder the Zelda-themed Switch 2, and the gift card "essentially grants what sounds like a free Switch 2".

Based on some other customer stories online, Walmart may also be offering "one or the other", where the customer gets to either reorder the limited edition system or can get a gift card matching the cost of this unit.

#4107. BioWare staff "should be given the first opportunity and the federal support" to buy the studio and keep it running, says Canadian political party leader

Hope. It's in short supply at the moment. Regardless, I hope that something a Canadian politician's proposed in a post scoring easy likeability points at the expense of EA's recently installed owners comes to pass, no matter how unlikely it is to do so at this point. Rather than being unceremoniuously shuttered, leaving the world staring down the barrel of a future without new games from a storied studio, BioWare should be handed over to its staff with backing from the Canadian government.

Nationalise BioWare, basically. Well, sort of. "The developers at BioWare know how to run the studio," is what Avi Lewis, leader of Canada's New Democratic Party, wrote in a post following the closure. "They know how to make the games we all love. They should be given the first opportunity - and the federal support - to buy it and run it themselves. And if we want to avoid the Mass Effect effect in Canada, we should be keeping private equity out, not welcoming it in."

You can almost hear the horde of suit-wearing money-knowers who've sensed that suggestion's been made and are about to descend from orbit to yell about taxpayers' money being used to help ensure the creation of future adventures starring space blokes who say 'We'll bang, ok?'. I should also point out that since I'm not Canadian, it wouldn't be the country I live in spending some of their cash on helping the Veilguard avoid being veilgone to the depths of the vault where EA keep Burnout and ten million other defunct series people would like to see return.

The developers at BioWare know how to run the studio. They know how to make the games we all love. They should be given the first opportunity - and the federal support - to buy it and run it themselves.

In all seriousness, I'm not totally sure it'd work out in the long run, but it's something. An alternative to a company erasing a studio from existence because the Saudi Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushner have been allowed to load them up with a ton of debt rather than reaching further into their own pockets.

So, I say screw it. Set up a new position called Minister for BioWare to ensure the devs have what they need to get their heads down that next Mass Effect which reportedly had a trailer leak the other day. Just make sure it's not some right-wing crank, or BioWare might run into some of the same problems it'd been feared their generally very inclusive games might face under Saudi ownership.

#4105. Future? No Thanks! dev removes AI-generated voices from game and offers refunds to players who feel "betrayed"

Next game will be"completely hand-coded".

Open world ecosatire Future? No Thanks! has been updated to remove some AI-generated voices, after lead developer Paolo "Molleindustria" Pedercini belatedly disclosed his usage of the technology earlier this week. He's also offering to refund people over Paypal or Venmo if they "still feel betrayed" by this.

The update removes two instances of text-to-speech generated voicework for in-game robot characters – an automated toilet and an automated translator in a hair salon. In his previous blog, Pedercini wrote that he used genAI for these characters as a spoof of generative AI. He's decided to replace them with human voice-acting following a number of angry reactions on social media and some coverage in the press.

"The voices were recorded earlier this year but I decided to not use them because I thought the actual uncanny text-to-speech was funnier in that context," Pedercini writes in a new blog post. "Alas, the new generation of text-to-speech counts as user-facing AI-generated content and that keeps creating all sorts of annoyances and bad optics."

Pedercini still thinks the text-to-speech voices belong in Future? No Thanks! "In my opinion the game is worse now, but only, like, 0.001% worse," he observes. In less acrimonious tidings, he's also tweaked the game so that the "various gigs give you a bit more money, possibly preventing some situations of soft-locking players from achieving all the quests."

The blog includes a "personal update" in which Pedercini expounds rather bitterly upon the backlash to the game's genAI elements. "Somebody from Bluesky (the Twitter/X clone) dragged me due to a post disclosing what I foolishly thought a minor use of generative-AI in Future? No Thanks!" he writes. "I gave versions of that statement multiple times before, whenever asked by festivals and events. Steam doesn’t require disclosure of generative AI for things like code assistance so many people assume their favorite indie games don’t use AI at all just because the developers stay mum."

For context, Valve updated Steam's rules in January to allow "efficiency" tools, such as coding assistants. I'm basing this on anecdotes and conversations with other devs, rather than any kind of statistical survey, but it seems very likely that a lot of developers on Steam aren't disclosing their genAI use - the policy has always been more of a gesture on Valve's part than a mechanism of real accountability.

"Not me, I’m a good boy and I wanted a page I could link to that explains that NO, this is not a vibecoded slop game but YES, I did ask chatGPT to fix a broken shader and a few things like that," Pedercini goes on. "More foolishly, I added a paragraph that sounded like I was trying to exculpate myself by poo-pooing on all the colleagues that advocate for an AI-free life." (The paragraph in collection was deleted after the original blog's publication, but not before it had been screengrabbed and shared on the socials.)

"Look, it was not a good post," Pedercini concedes. "Defeatist, hastily written. I thought nobody would read it. Anyway, slow news day, everybody fucking hates AI, the whole scene piled on."

Pedercini proceeds to caricature some of the people yelling at him over social media: "Am I satirizing the puppy killing machine by KILLING PUPPIES?" He compares the anger he's received to being harrassed by Adam Baldwin's followers at the height of the Gamergate hate campaign.

Pedercini ends by sharing a list of developers who've sworn off generative AI. "Big props to them," he writes. "Give them a follow. SteamFest is drowning in actual slop, help them stand out. And I hate to break it to you, but you should probably assume that all the studios that have not made a public statement against all generative AI are using it for coding in some capacity. I’m guessing this episode isn’t going to encourage more voluntary disclosures." As for his next game, it'll be "completely hand-coded".

As IT: Welcome to Derry season 2 stays in preproduction, HBO keeps fans fed with a secret Halloween episode

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Do you remember when Stranger Things fans convinced themselves that a secret ninth episode was on the way earlier this year? Well, although we never did get to go back to Hawkins, another beloved franchise has taken its fanbase by surprise and delivered a secret instalment, allowing fans to return back to Derry almost one year after IT: Welcome to Derry season 1 came to an end.

Without any warning, HBO randomly released the 30-minute-long bonus episode, titled 'A Story of Derry,' on Halloween. Set hundreds of years before Pennywise came to be, the new episode follows three youngsters from a Native American tribe who venture into the Western Wood where they encounter a terrifying ancient spirit. HBO Max shared a short trailer for the special on Twitter, which you can watch below.

IT's a surprise Halloween treat. Catch this never-before-seen special exploring the origins of IT in Derry. #AStoryOfDerry is streaming now on HBO Max. 🎈 https://t.co/NH3NcMLt8nOctober 31, 2026

The new episode gives us more insight into what the evil entity we know as IT actually is and why it targets Derry. However, we got a little taste of this in IT: Welcome to Derry season 1. In episode 4, after Dick Hallorann enters Taniel's mind, he learns that the Native Americans stumbled upon the entity, which they call 'Tha Gallo,' many years ago when they settled on the land. Tha Gallo murdered tribe members and would grow stronger with every kill, so the natives imprisoned it beneath a large area that would later become the town of Derry.

The special brings Dick's vision to life and reveals just how the natives caged the beast. We already know that the spirit was kept at bay by a number of pillars placed around the forest, which is why it can never leave Derry and break out into the wider world. However, the caveat is that IT wakes every 27 years and causes a catastrophic event in Derry before it sleeps again. IT: Welcome to Derry season 1 takes place in the '60s, 27 years before the first IT movie, which in turn takes place 27 years before IT: Chapter 2.

IT: Welcome to Derry season 2 is set to take us right back to the 1930s. Just as season 1 saw the monster feed on the horrific Black Spot disaster, season 2 is set around another tragic event: the Bradley Gang Massacre. Mentioned in Stephen King's 1986 novel, the event sees a band of criminals target stores and banks in Derry, which leads to a deadly shootout in the middle of town. Season 2 is currently in the pre-production stage, with Crystal Lake creator Brad Caleb Kane serving as solo showrunner this time.

It: Welcome to Derry season 2 does not yet have a release date. For more, check out our list of the best shows on HBO Max, and keep up with upcoming Stephen King movies and shows on the way.

#4103. Factorio's final major update has rolled off the assembly line, adding "the things we wanted to do for 2.0 but didn't have time for"

Including QoL tweaks, new visuals, and more predictable asteroids

In one of the happier endings to occur in games this week, impossibly enormous resource management sim Factorio has just released its last-ever major update – version 2.1 – on its stable branch. As previously heads-upped by developers Wube Software, 2.1 doesn’t make any big new additions to its planets or tech trees, but does sneak in more than 30 quality of life improvements and minor new features for both the base game and its Space Age expansion. Including, they say, "the things we wanted to do for 2.0 but didn't have time for." Nice to get a few final pieces out the door before it closes, eh.

There’s also an updated trailer, if you want to watch promotional footage for a game that may well have enveloped your every waking moment since 2016.

Factorio - Trailer 2026 Watch on YouTube

Here are some of those changes I’ve picked out at random. "Mixed rockets: Rockets can now carry multiple different items in one launch, so no more sending a full stack of everything just to build a small platform." Nice! "Land mines can be used as tripwires and enemy detectors." Devious! "Asteroid damage now depends on the asteroid's remaining health instead of its speed, so it is much more predictable." Convenient! Not counting how you’re still being hit by an asteroid. There’s also now the ability to play Space Age without the controversial Quality mechanic, as well as the ability to flip pumpjacks and burner miners instead of merely rotating them, like some loser.

The 2.1 update also gives Factorio one last graphical polish, including a handful of new models and a "new pump rendering system that can connect to fluid wagons no matter how cursed your station is." I’m merely pretending to be a Factorio expert for the purposes of publishing this article, though I will say – from experience building piplines in Deep Rock Galactic – that a series of tubes is only truly cursed if it still works, in spite of itself, at transporting liquids. Otherwise you’ve just got a pile of broken pipes, again, like some loser.

This isn’t the end-end of Factorio, which Wube Software have said will continue to get bug fixes and support-level updates while they largely move on to "other game prototypes/experiments." Though even if it was, it’s had a bloomin' admirable run, starting with four years of early access - successful enough to cement it as the de facto basis for later automation-builders like Satisfactory and Dyson Sphere Program – and continuing to enrapture aspiring industrial managers into the present. Ollie has over 1,000 hours in it. Maybe I’m the loser for making light of it.

#4101. Hardware Review: SCUF Omega PS5 Controller - No-Frills Pro Controller Doesn't Do Much to Impress

For the last few weeks, I’ve been testing out the SCUF Omega PlayStation controller, a highly customisable pro controller ideal for those looking to step up their competitive play. With a plethora of additional buttons and a high price tag to go with it, let’s see if the Omega is worth your time.

Please note that some external links on this page are affiliate links, which means if you click them and make a purchase we may receive a small percentage of the sale. Please read our FTC Disclosure for more information.

The SCUF Omega is an officially licenced pro controller compatible with both PS5 and PC. It is able to connect with the PS5 via either a wired connection or wirelessly thanks to a dongle. It also has Bluetooth connectivity for PCs.

It retails for £209.99/$219.99, but can go up to £229.99/$229.99 depending on your customisation options.

The SCUF Omega unboxing is a no-frills experience. With a PlayStation-branded box, you’re treated to a sort of rough fabric hard case, inside of which there is the controller, its dongle, and a nice braided USB-A to C charging cable.

The style of the SCUF Omega is probably one of its best features, as this thing can be highly customised on the SCUF website. There are a series of prebuilt options, but you can really get into the weeds, choose face-button colours, thumbsticks and even the touchpad design. Some of these will bump the price up by another £20.

For our unit, we were sent the Cherry Blossom design. I’m not going to lie, it’s not the design I would have picked, but I suppose it shows off the breadth of designs available.

Picking up the controller for the first time, I wasn’t really struck by any one thing. It’s a controller. It’s fairly light, but not so light that it feels cheap, nor heavy enough that it feels expensive. The rubber grips on the back mean it is comfortably secure in the hand. Overall, however, it doesn’t make any particularly strong first impressions.

There’s a nice smooth travel to the triggers, and the face buttons have a really satisfying mouse click effect, which can also be applied to the triggers with a switch on the back.

Thumbsticks are smooth with TMR, or Tunnelling Magnetoresistance, to ensure stick drift isn’t an issue here, and SCUF claims higher accuracy over Hall Effect sticks.

The extra buttons in this case are four rear paddles, and oddly, a button on each side of the controller. There is also a series of five buttons at the bottom of the controller which are a mix of programmable buttons and volume and mic controls.

As is custom for controllers like this, it doesn’t feature any form of rumble or adaptive triggers.

Connecting and customising the SCUF Omega is a fairly straightforward process.

To connect to the PS5, either plugging in the wired connection or dongle in will pretty much do it. Although, interestingly, there is a rather awkward switch under the faceplate that you must switch to if you want to use a dongle connection as opposed to Bluetooth or wired, and the same is the case when switching from PS5 to PC connectivity. It’s not difficult to do – the faceplates have snap magnets, making it super easy to swap out – but it feels like a bit of a tedious step.

Customising the controller is done via an app on either your PC or mobile. This again is fairly straightforward. You can save three profiles to switch between, which is handy for me as someone who has one controller set for a game like The Finals and another for a game like Modern Warfare 4.

You can switch out the input for any button on the controller and change thumbstick deadzones, meaning there is a lot to experiment with here.

Once you’ve connected and customised, how does it feel to play? Well, for me, this was a mixed bag.

On the one hand, I really appreciated the snappy responsiveness of the clicky face buttons and the trigger customisation, which made it brilliant for fast-paced FPS games. Those TMR thumbsticks also feel right at home, as they don’t have that lack of resistance you find in Hall Effect sticks.

On the other hand, I found many of the additional buttons a bit awkward to use. The side buttons in particular are super easy to press accidentally, and the back paddles are a little finicky, especially compared to a controller like the DualSense Edge.

Ultimately, I found that the controller was actually a little small in my hands too, which meant I was having to twist and turn my hands to actually hit those buttons, as opposed to them naturally being where my fingers sit. I’d never go as far as saying my hands were cramping, but they were slightly uncomfortable.

To be fair, I do have slightly larger hands, so this may be a non-issue for some, but I just never particularly gelled with this controller in practice. I felt like to really get the most out of this controller, I'd need to be put in the training to finally sync up with it, as opposed to it just working with me straight out of the box.

It’s tough for me to fully recommend the SCUF Omega. It’s a controller that just does what it says on the tin, with no weird features or gimmicks. For that reason, I respect its simplicity.

Customising the inputs is easy and quick, you can customise the controller design when buying so it suits your style, and many of the standard elements like triggers, thumbstick, and face buttons feel nice.

However, considering you’re parting with over 200 clams for this thing, I personally would like my controller to feel a bit more premium. Its additional customisation options also make it feel like a controller you need to adapt to, rather than a controller that just feels right.

For some, that’s a non-issue, and I’m sure many players looking to step up their game will be able to do so with this controller. But for me, it doesn’t do enough to pull me away from the controllers I’m already using.

Have you picked up the SCUF Omega? What did you think of its design? Customise those buttons and head down to the comment section below.

#4099. Round Up: The Reviews Are In For Stellar Blade's Switch 2 Port

It's all about Link this week, but there is another notable release arriving for the Switch 2 on the same day. It's Shift Up's action game, Stellar Blade.

We've already taken a look at the port here on Nintendo Life, and despite some drawbacks, Eve's outing stands tall on the hybrid platform. Here's how we summed it up:

"Despite some drawbacks, Stellar Blade stands tall as an impressive and enjoyable action game that occupies a nice niche in the Switch 2 library. Rewarding exploration, thrilling combat, and tough but fair difficulty carry this game far and make it an easy recommendation, even if its story can be a bit bland and the visuals aren’t always up to the task."

Review Stellar Blade: Complete Edition (Switch 2) - Perfectly Playable, Despite Drawbacks

So, what did other critics have to say? Read on to find out...

"Stellar Blade is one of the best action adventure titles to release in the current console generation. Comparisons to NieR: Automata and Bayonetta are inevitable (particularly with the DLC costumes to highlight the similarities), but mostly only down to shared aesthetics and some thematic similarities with the former, as the game carves out its own unique identity with its superb combat. The visual cuts are there, and it is absolutely unplayable with frame generation enabled, but with some slight tweaks to the default settings, it delivers a fantastic experience on Nintendo Switch 2 – particularly in handheld mode."

"Stellar Blade Complete Edition is a shining testament to what developers with the right know-how can achieve on Switch 2. Shift Up has clearly taken this project very seriously and they’re out to not only expand the reach of their IP, but also flaunt their technical chops. Having poured a ton of time into Stellar Blade Complete Edition"

"All told, Stellar Blade Complete Edition on Nintendo Switch 2 is a great way to experience Shift Up’s action game ahead of the series’ next entry. It might have some graphical blemishes on Nintendo’s comparatively underpowered hardware, but those blemishes don’t quite matter during the moment-to-moment, adrenaline-pumping gameplay that Stellar Blade delivers in spades."

"The Switch 2 version of Stellar Blade is competent but struggles to hit the same heights as the original. With its steady framerate, the game runs extremely well both docked and handheld. While it’s incredible that Shift Up has managed to get the game working on Nintendo’s latest hardware, some compromises have been made. Animations dip at a distance and the game isn’t as responsive as the original. It may not be the best version of the game, but it remains a worthwhile option for those who want to experience EVE’s adventure on the go."

"If you haven’t played this Korean hit, or want it on Nintendo consoles, now is the perfect opportunity. It includes Nier Automata and Goddess of Victory: Nikke DLCs, updates, and quality-of-life improvements. Properly optimized for Nintendo Switch 2, this port is an example of what developers can do when they set their minds to it. The exclusive Bayonetta DLC costumes are the icing on this cake. It does not apologize for being sexy and wears it with pride and honor. A game for fans and the consumer’s joy and awe. An example of what games can and should strive for."

News Stellar Blade's Switch 2 Release Will Include A Frame Generation Toggle

So will you be making time for Eve this week? Let us know in the comments.

Liam is a news writer and reviewer on Nintendo Life. He's been writing about games for more than 15 years and is a lifelong fan of many iconic video game characters.

#4098. Mass Effect 3 ending discourse ignored the RPG's scale, ambition, and exuberance, including that of its oddly great co-op

Ah, come on, it was fine. Better than fine. We can argue for another fourteen years about whether BioWare should have redone the ending or not, but Mass Effect 3 was really a compendium of endings, a ludicrously ambitious wrapping-up of dozens of plot threads, character arcs, and running gags. Even if you can point to other RPGs that, on an individual basis, are more branching and reactive, Mass Effect 3's largely successful closing of a galaxy's worth of choose-your-own adventure books - filled in and followed across three evolving instalments - showed an audacity and grandiosity that no other three-part series had matched before. Or, at least on that scale, has pulled off since.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

It didn't hurt that Mass Effect 3 also had the trilogy's fiercest, bangiest action by far, nor some of its highest-stakes, often most lip-chewing moments of decisionmaking. It is true that the accumulation of War Assets wasn't always as heavy on character drama as the game-long preparation for Mass Effect 2's Suicide Mission, but then you don't simply play Mass Effect 3 to make a number go higher. You play it to punch or hug reporters, to love or shoot your friends, to save or damn entire species. And it has loads of that, right up to the point to have to choose the colour of an explosion. Potentially beyond, if you treat the (assuredly, delightfully) fanservice-forward Citadel expansion as Shepard's true last ride.

Back in 2013, and again with 2021's Legendary Edition, I was sad that Mass Effect 3 ended and glad that it happened. That, at the risk of appearing less furious at EA's stewardship than I am, does not change with BioWare's closure. What does bother me is the uncertainty over what now happens to Mass Effect 3's surprisingly entertaining, weirdly long-lived co-op mode.

I don't doubt this was put in for boring, C-suite, "gamers want multiplayer" reasons. But that only gave the resultant palled-up superpower maelstroms a sense that they were better than they had any right to be, with explosive moments of player-to-player power synergies and spacious, blindspot-filled maps that could maintain a thrilling feeling of being permanently surrounded. Post-release additions to the species-spanning character roster also showed glimpses of that same, fuck-it swagger that BioWare exhibited in the campaign, as they increasingly moved away from familiar soldier archtypes towards electric whip wielders, regenerating lizards, teleporting ninjas, and three-foot-tall psychic asthmatics. While many of today's co-op shooters fret over miniscule balance changes, in pursuit of some mythically perfect meta, Mass Effect 3's gave you a crate of action figures and told you to go nuts.

While I haven't played it recently, there's a small but loyal contingent who do, and for their sake I hope the multiplayer's P2P setup helps it survive the EA cull. I was, and for now technically still is, too good to be doomed to oblivion. Or, worse, vibe-coded Legendary Edition mods.

#4097. Edgar Wright says 4K AI remaster of Spaced releasing next year is "not authorized by anyone involved in making the show"

A 4K remaster of Spaced is on the way, but Edgar Wright doesn't approve

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new 4K remaster of classic British comedy series Spaced is on the way, but it seems like someone wished for it on a monkey's paw, as it's been upscaled using "algorithmic corrections" and none of the show's original creators are involved, including Edgar Wright.

Responding to a fan on X, Wright confirmed that the 4K release of Spaced, which is currently up for pre-order on Amazon UK, was news to him and fellow Spaced alumni, like Simon Pegg and Nick Frost. "Finding out about this for the first time is... disheartening," Wright posted on X. "I had been pushing to do a Blu-Ray of SPACED for years, so to find out that someone just went ahead without our involvement is.... a bummer. Not authorized by anyone involved in making the show. Finding out what happened as we speak…"

To make matters worse, the Amazon listing confirms that the show, which ran from 1999-2001 and was shot on standard definition DigiBeta cameras, was upscaled to 4K using a proprietary AI algorithm. British label All3 Media is behind the release.

"This global first Blu-Ray collection," reads the Amazon listing, "has been upgraded to a brand new 4K master using a combination of traditional and proprietary tools in a multi-step process of non-commercial and algorithmic corrections that are additionally enhanced frame by frame by a manual operator – guaranteeing the most state-of-the-art upconversion possible." That's a whole lot of words not to say AI…

Spaced was one of the early great DVD boxsets, featuring hours of special features involving Cornetto trilogy pals Wright, Pegg, Frost and many famous fans (Diablo Cody, Kevin Smith and Matt Stone all contribute to the commentary tracks), but for reasons currently unclear, this new edition won't feature any new contributions from those who made it.

"It’s a Channel 4 show," Wright pointed out when asked how this could happen without his knowledge. "We were all very involved in the previous editions, but not this one."

The 4K remaster of Spaced releases on February 27, 2027 in the UK, though whether you'll want to pick it up is another question. As for Wright, we don't know what the Baby Driver and Last Night in Soho director is working on next, though his partner in crime Simon Pegg did confirm earlier this year that he and Wright are working on a new film together, telling Something About Rocks, "Edgar and I are, at the moment, meeting up weekly either in person or on Zoom, just to talk about ideas. We’ve got a lot of potential avenues to walk down."

Spaced can currently be streamed on Channel 4 in the UK. For more, dive into our list of upcoming TV shows or upcoming movies.

#4096. I've got egg on my face because Steam's Personal Calendar feature has apparently been a test this whole time and is only now actually a fully fledged component

I'll be honest folks: I didn't know that Steam's Personal Calendar feature was still technically in testing. I've been using it here and there to keep track of what's come out recently or what's coming out imminently, and have generally found it to be fairly reflective of the kinds of games I was interested in. It just worked! Yet lo and behold, a post from Valve went out yesterday announcing that the feature has launched out of Steam Labs "and is considered a full feature of the Steam Store."

The feature, if you've missed it, is "another way to see recommended games for you, showing both recently released and upcoming games filtered down to the set of games we think you are most likely to be interested in," as Valve explain it anyway. "It uses your recently played games to find people with similar playtime profiles to you, and then looks at the games those players have been adding to their wishlist or playing." I do wonder if there's a bit more going under the hood here, as my playtime count is all over the place, with nothing above 50 hours on there, and that's an exception to the norm (I'm from more of a console background, alright).

But even still, my recommendations do remain pretty good, showing me games that I have since added to my wishlist. I'm never opposed to new discovery tools, especially considering how bad Valve can actually be at that kind of thing. Apparently the recommendation system refreshes daily "to incorporate the latest data. In reality you aren't likely to see your recommendations change all that much from day to day, but as time goes by you will obviously see new things pop up as the 8-week horizon of the calendar marches forward, or as games lock in their release dates."

This comes as part of a broader swathe of changes Valve have been introducing to Steam over the past couple of years, including one from last month that will change its homepage discounts and events section to be a bit more algorithm based. Perhaps it's some kind of weird prepwork for that new Half-Life they're almost definitely making but only talk about accidentally.

#4095. Paralives' first major update slips to next year, but when it comes you can expect some pretty meaty improvements for all of its main features

Since launch back in May of this year, life sim Paralives appears to have been trucking along nicely, with the dev team offering up fairly regular updates with all sorts of tweaks big and small. Certainly confidence-inspiring for an early access game, especially one as systems-driven as it is. And now, the Paralives team have outlined their plans for the game's first major update, which seem very catered to improving the core experience.

As part of a four point plan they outlined, first up on the docket is "buffing up the basics." This is all about strengthening some of the currently existing Live Mode systems. That means improvements to how relationships function by unlocking more things when a relationship level goes up, adding in more interactions that change your Para's emotions, improving the Community Centre's bundles and tweaking the economy curve so it isn't as easy to get money.

The next point is on expanding the Live Mode, meaning the addition of a pair of new skills, adding in more together and story cards, new relationship label unlockables, and more jobs too. Build Mode will also see some improvements, with a big focus on build breaking bugs. You can also expect new bits of furniture and items, and a tweak to furniture and item efficiency.

Lastly, there are also planned improvements to the Paramaker. One is by adding in more hairstyles and clothing items, notably baggy outfits, and the other is increasing the range of fat and muscle sliders "to represent a wider variety of body shapes." As a bigger person myself I'm always enthused when character creators actually let you have a fat body, so this is a welcome point from the dev team.

Worth noting that this list "is not final," and some things may be pushed back with others getting added in. Also worth noting is that while this first major update was planned for the end of 2026, it's been pushed into next year as the team needs a bit more time. You can read about all of these plans in more detail over on Steam.

#4094. HELENA : Cloud District is a megastructure photography game laser targeted at my interests, and it's out next week

Yes, I'm doing it, I'm writing about a megastructure game for the second time this week because come on, HELENA : Cloud District just looks stunning, don't it? Admittedly there's a chance you've not heard of it, that be the way of things in this algorithmically dominated world, but allow me to tell you about its big, scary world and the strange camera you're equipped with to capture all the sights it holds.

In the world of HELENA : Cloud District, you have come across a rotting megastructure that appears to be long abandoned, all sorts of strange flora dotted throughout it. In one part, it's something of a precision first-person platformer, as you navigate its intricately layered world with drops so steep you'd probably die before you hit the bottom. At the centre of it all is a computer, and it's here where you must bring all of your photographs in order to learn more about the history of the place.

The in-game camera itself is a fascinating thing to look at, completely impossible, alien and ancient in its design. From what I can tell it's a sort of metallic helmet, these insect-like segments snapping into place when you're gearing up to take a snap. You only appear to have three photo slots at any given point in time, meaning you can't just go gallivanting around the place all trigger happy like. There's an amount of care you have to put in positioning yourself and subsequently finding your way back to the central computer.

It's non-linear too, there's no set path you have to take, and it seems like there's some neat movement mechanics too. "Slide, hover, and glide through the structure in your own creative way in order to reach every level and get deeper into the slumbering Cloud District," explains the game's Steam page. Sounds like you don't have to worry too much about that falling to your death thing, then. I'm quite enthused by what HELENA : Cloud District is putting down, and it has a release date now too: October 29th. Same day as Hypnos! I now dub October 29th megastructure day. There will not be a vote on this matter. Ahead of HELENA's release, make sure to give it a wishlist on Steam.

#4092. Fortnite's Pirate Shop Unlocks the Entire Item Shop for Free

Battle Royale tops five million concurrent players

In case you haven’t been paying attention, Fortnite is running a pirate-themed season with One Piece crossover content available right now.

But the big news is the discovery of a Pirate Shop, which makes the entire Item Shop free for two weeks. If you’re running in a squad, then everyone on your team gets the reward.

Just to reiterate: if you discover the Pirate Shop token, then you and your teammates will be able to add every single cosmetic item in the Item Shop to your profile for free. That’s potentially hundreds of dollars of stuff.

There are some restrictions: you can’t gift anything to your friends, and you can’t buy levels in the Battle Pass. Other than that, though – everything is yours.

In the aftermath of the Pirate Shop going viral, Fortnite rocketed to over five million concurrent players across all platforms at its peak. It’s a big win for the game which hasn’t been quite as popular as usual of late.

Some are hypothesising that this may be the game’s attempt to retain players once GTA 6 releases later in November. I imagine it’s something all live service developers are thinking about.

So how do you get access to the Pirate Shop? Well, you need to loot Treasure-Hunt chests (they’ve got a skull and crossbones on them) and hope you get extremely lucky. I imagine Epic knows how many of these it’s giving out.

I’m surprised something like this hasn’t been attempted in Fortnite before, because the game’s skins are incredibly popular, so unlocking the Item Shop for lucky winners was always going to bring people back.

I’ll be surprised if anyone here gets access to the Pirate Shop, but make sure you leave a comment if you do!

#4091. Feature: 25 Years Later, How Many Of These Original Xbox Launch Titles Have You Played?

From the original North American launch on November 15, 2001

Welcome to the month of Xbox's 25th anniversary! Xbox will be celebrating that milestone officially on November 15th, but before we get there, we thought we'd use the chance to highlight the very first games that ever launched on Xbox.

To do that, we're going back to the initial list of North American Xbox launch titles, of which there were 20 in all. Some of them are obvious standouts, such as Halo: Combat Evolved, Fuzion Frenzy, Dead or Alive 3 and Project Gotham Racing, while others are more obscure - Arctic Thunder, Dark Summit, Mad Dash Racing, etc.

Here's the full list of all 20 launch titles:

Now, of course, some of these games are still playable to this day on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S, while others have always remained locked to the original Xbox. The likes of Project Gotham Racing, Shrek and Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2x are highly-requested additions to the Xbox backwards compatibility library, but it seems unlikely they'll ever make the cut at this point - almost certainly due to licensing reasons.

However, you may not know that games like Cel Damage and Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee are still playable to this day on modern consoles, and they're still well worth checking out despite their age.

So, how many of these original Xbox launch titles have you played? Let us know down in the comments section below, and please do give us your recommendations with some of the obscure ones - NHL Hitz is still one of my faves!

The closure of BioWare and cancellation of Mass Effect 5 that followed the EA buyout have understandably left countless longtime fans of the studio and RPG series distraught – so much so, in fact, some are expressing their disappointment physically.

You might already know about the Save Mass Effect petition, which has garnered hundreds of thousands of signatures worldwide and a plethora of strong supporters – including from fellow developers. It's safe to say that many folks are quite passionate about it, seeing as the wait between the fourth Mass Effect and Universe, as the fifth was confirmed to be called, has been nearly a decade in the making so far.So passionate, it seems, that they're taking to EA's offices with spray paint in hand. As one person over on Reddit spotted in Madrid, Spain, "#SaveMassEffect" graffiti is visible on the stone walls and ground surrounding EA.

Commenters see fans questioning whether this is the way to go about reviving the RPG, but it's actually not the only instance of people voicing (so to speak) their thoughts directly at the publisher's offices.

As a separate post on Twitter highlights, some fans are placing physical tombstones outside of EA in memory of BioWare – and other studios – reading "RIP." Underneath, you'll spot a Mass Effect quote: "It had to be me. Someone else might have gotten it wrong." It, admittedly, hits quite hard… and this example appears far more popular than the graffiti in Spain. As one comment reads, "Now this is good. We need more of this."

Fans have placed tombstones honoring the studios shut down by EA, including, of course, BioWare itself. The inscription on BioWare's tombstone reads: "Had to be me. Someone else might have gotten it wrong." #SaveMassEffect 💔 https://t.co/rNMMepTH1UNovember 1, 2026

Will it catch the attention of EA, though? I suppose only time will tell. And, as it stands now, it doesn't seem too likely that another publisher or company could swoop in and buy BioWare in hopes of saving the Mass Effect team. One former dev stated that "EA never actually sells anything" and we shouldn't expect a rekindling of Universe as "they just shut things down and sit on their licenses." I'm instantly reminded of American McGee's Alice, personally.

For the time being, I just hope that all affected devs are able to land on their feet. The fate of Mass Effect is certainly a sad one, but real people are struggling here as well amid all of the chaos – and that shouldn't be forgotten, either.

#4089. "System Shock and Deus Ex, they were RPGs. People called them RPGs": Gloomwood's publisher isn't too keen on using the term immersive sim despite it being one

You know, I think at this point in my life there is a non-zero chance I will die before anyone is able to settle comfortably on what defines an immersive sim. I'm not going to even try to! The idea is too annoying and I'm sure someone will disagree with some aspect of it. And if you ask New Blood boss Dave Oshry, when it comes to trying to flog an immersive sim, it's probably best to not even refer to it as one.

"Is it a good marketing term? No. It sucks," Oshry told PC Gamer in a recent interview. "It's awful." For those unfamiliar with New Blood, they're a publisher of some pretty cultishly popular games like ULTRAKILL, as well as immersive sims like Gloomwood and Fallen Aces. Ironically, though, it's through publishing Gloomwood and working with lead dev Dillon Rogers specifically that he even heard of the term. "He's like, 'That's what these are called'. I'm like, 'I have never heard that before in my life. What the fuck are you talking about?'"

That doesn't mean Oshry had never heard of or played an imsim before, he was familiar with classics like Deus Ex, he just considered them to be a different genre: RPGs. "System Shock and Deus Ex, they were RPGs. People called them RPGs. That's the funny thing about an immersive sim. You're immersed in this world. You're building your character. Yeah, that's called an RPG, brother. That's a roleplaying game." Perhaps a controversial statement amongst the diehard imsim fans, but perhaps not an entirely untrue statement either.

In Oshry's opinion, "if you market something as an RPG, I think you'll do better than marketing it as an immersive sim." This part I'm not sure I'd entirely agree with. Sure, everyone knows what an RPG is, but they do also have certain expectations that come with them, such as stats and the like that you don't typically find in imsims. Ahah! Maybe that's the difference. Immersive sims are RPGs without the stats. By golly, I've done it without even trying. Either way, this Oshry fellow does seem to be pretty good at peddling weird little indies, so maybe I should just pipe down.

#4088. Abelina is a strange, platforming romp through a natural afterlife from a former League of Legends animator and the composer of Zach Cregger's Resident Evil

Would that make what we're currently in the beforedeath?

I have no particular thoughts on what the afterlife may look like, namely because if there is one, and I'm allowed to hang out in it, I don't want to be disappointed. What if I have the expectation that it's a hedonistic paradise and am met with only having a guy named Gary who only eats cheese sandwiches for company? How embarrassing! No, I'll leave the imagining to others on this particular front. Doing so bears some ripe fruit for me occasionally, too, as is the case today with Abelina, a surreal platformer about a man who died and finds himself tending to gardens and carving masks and trying "not to think about what this place might really be."

My immediate reaction upon seeing Abelina is that it has the vibe of a Soviet stop motion film only Letterboxd users have heard of, which is perhaps the highest compliment I can give to a game graphically. In it, you play as Vasily, who "died a while ago." He finds himself in the titular Abelina, an odd, nature-filled afterlife, where he's been trying to find happiness again with a small handful of other folks doing the same.

I don't think Abelina is a puzzle game, but it does look like you have to put some thought into your platforming at points. There is flying to be done, dungbeetle-esque rolling, precise jumps to be made. It seems the entire thing is about navigating this otherworldly locale, and hopefully finding some truth amongst it all. You may not always find the correct path, with branching paths and open vistas seemingly offering a multitude of ways forward, all while being led by a "mysterious rabbit-cat."

It's also a game with some skill behind it, being led by Gabe Askew, who's worked on CG cinematics for the likes of Valorant, League of Legends and Love, Death + Robots. Sonically we should be in for a pleasant time too, as Weapons and the recent Resident Evil movie's composer Ryan Holladay is on the soundtrack for Abelina. I'm curious about what else it has to offer and am keen to get my hands on it to see how that platforming feels. In the meantime, you might join me by wishlisting it on Steam ahead of its release in 2027.

NetEase reportedly pulled funding earlier this year

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nagoshi Studio – the developer founded by Yakuza and Super Monkey Ball creator Toshihiro Nagoshi – has been shut down.

Following the release of series semi-reboot Yakuza: Like a Dragon and Lost Judgement, Nagoshi departed Sega after an over 30-year career at the company, founding Nagoshi Studio alongside Yakuza series director Daisuke Sato. The NetEase studio remained pretty quiet until The Game Awards in 2025 where its debut title Gang of Dragon was unveiled with a trailer starring Train to Busan and soon-to-be Physint star Ma Dong-seok.

Earlier this year, reports emerged that NetEase was pulling funding on the game after reportedly discovering it would need an extra 7 billion yen in funding, following the developer's YouTube channel and website being taken down, as well as Sato changing his Twitter bio to say ex-Nagoshi Studio, leaving the game and studio's future in doubt. Now, just over five years since Nagoshi left Sega, a notice posted in Japanese government gazette Kanpo (via Gematsu) confirms that Nagoshi Studio was dissolved on October 31.

NetEase has been pulling back on investments over the last year or two, with Worlds Untold – founded by Mass Effect writer Mac Walters – and Jar of Sparks – founded by former Halo lead Jerry Hooks – having their funding pulled. Meanwhile, Suda 51-founded Grasshopper Manufacture self-published its most recent title – Romeo Is a Dead Man – despite being owned by NetEase, with the studio splitting from the publisher to go independent just over a month ago.

Neither Nagoshi or the studio has been active on social media since the start of the year, so no official word has been made by the developer.

#4086. The Sunday Papers

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

Sundays are, again, for running taxi duty for relatives visiting from overseas. If I had a nickel for every time I had an early morning Gatwick run in tandem with a Sunday Papers post, I’d have two nickels, which isn’t a lot but it’s weird than I’m being paid in USD when I live in the United Kingdom. In that international spirit, here are some fine writings from around the globe.

For Stop Caring, Artemis Octavio interviewed Jeremy Couillard, the multimedia artist behind such offbeat indie experiments as Soul Injector Commando: an FPS about shooting a sense of humanity into enemies based on real-life billionaires.

This past week’s discourse on gamedev team sizes, sparked by a GI.biz post about Star Wars: Galactic Racer and its "core team" of 75, was clearly an inferior rehash of the Nic-sparked Expedition 33 one last year. But it has produced this thoughtful Game Developer piece, by Bryant Francis, on whether we need a new language approach to fit recent developments in outsourcing.

When done right, the model diversifies financial risk and preserves what works about triple-A development without the need to keep everyone under one corporate entity. When done wrong, you can wind up with a game development class system, where creative direction and funding flows in limited directions, and those not lucky enough to be at the center struggle to keep doing the work they love.

This problem is obviously organizational in nature, and not easily fixed by good copyediting. But organizations begin with language, and the language we use to define our work will define the future of video game development.

Writer and former Double Finer Harper Jay considers when games fail. In the interesting 'intent and aspirations' sense, not the tedious 'sales and Steam player counts' sense.

Manhunt’s investment into the stealth simulation is not insignificant, especially for the time. Even with the conceit that there is a snuff director engineering these scenarios, it wants you to understand that there is a world. It behaves largely as you might expect. The rules are mostly the rules of the real worlds. a brick falls because there is "gravity" and it makes "noise" like a normal brick would.

But! There’s rules to the game. Do X and a guard will do Y. Exploiting this is a key to progress and getting high scores. hit a wall, the mook says the thing, he walks over. this is the rule. at least so far.

But this guy doesn’t move. It’s not some meta-textual commentary, it’s not some undercutting trick on the player. He’s just not programmed that way. So I mention it to the game club. something’s up.

This doesn’t work. It doesn’t align. The simulation fails. The artifice is too obvious here. The funhouse is on display a bit too brazenly. It’s endearing maybe in the way that all jank can be. but it’s "off."

Eurogamer’s Robert Purchese meets the man who put a Game Boy Museum into a Game Boy cartridge.

I’ve been learning, as I recommend you do, about the eccentric American moneyman Timothy Dexter (1747-1806), whose preternatural luck in seeing his bumbling investments succeed was matched only by his zest for unhinged wordsmithing. Not really a 'from this week', of course. But then I only heard about the guy on Tuesday after Edwin, mad with fury after years of me editing commas into his articles, sent me Dexter’s punctuation sheet supplement, which he included in reprints of one work “Nowing ones complane of my book the fust edition had no stops”.

I did look around for something BioWare-related to include here, but to be perfectly honest I still think the best eulogy I've read is Edwin's. Even if the first draft needed some commas. Music this week is alternating between Clutch’s gigantic, dive-bombing Wasted Lands, and this SilvaGunner remix of Unbeatable’s best song. Good Sundays, all.

#4085. OG Xbox Game 'Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee' Gets Remastered, But What Do The Critics Think?

Was it worth digging the original Xbox title back up?

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee launched on the original Xbox in 2003, a few months after its GameCube debut, and sadly, only in North America. The kaiju arena-brawler, which depicted the iconic King of Monsters, Godzilla, body-slamming Ghidorah into various cityscapes, has apparently made a big enough impact to warrant Atari funding a remaster in 2026.

Sadly, the whole North American release made it quite difficult for us Brits to get our mucky mitts on the game, and DAMM wasn't a big enough deal for Xbox to share the game with the rest of the world. DAMM did get the backward compatibility treatment, however, only on Xbox 360, and again restricted to North America.

I guess then, we're quite pleased Atari decided to take a punt on a DAMM remaster. Even though it seems to share many of the original's downfalls, Godzilla's WWE antics are going to be available on November 3rd on Xbox Series X|S, and best of all, I can play it from my lovely little home in Cornwall.

So, here's what the critics are saying about Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered:

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered brings the classic kaiju brawler roaring back with impressive rebuilt visuals, satisfying arena destruction, and chaotic multiplayer battles. While its limited roster and tedious character unlocks feel dated, the accessible combat and faithful Godzilla presentation make this a thoroughly entertaining return for the King of the Monsters."

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered feels like a new game with its graphical upgrade, held back slightly by a lack of any other meaningful new additions and a somewhat grindy gameplay loop."

"Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a satisfyingly faithful update to a beloved Kaiju brawler. It’s simple and fun, with local and online multiplayer keeping you around for the long haul despite a wafer-thin single-player experience. Now if we could just get a remaster of Save The Earth and Unleashed."

Review Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered (Switch 2) - The King Returns With A Fun But Thin Kaiju Brawler

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is at its best when it simulates the idea of smashing kaiju toys together as a kid in short sessions with friends, and at its worst when it attempts to prolong a game that never had much depth to begin with. The result is a remaster I’m glad exists considering the drought of Godzilla brawlers, but with a few caveats–not to mention the sting of realizing that the original GameCube and Xbox game were absent of arbitrary grinding."

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered remains goofy fun, and Atari’s remaster looks and runs well. It’s still a rather simple game and probably not the most comprehensive when it comes to the characters and lore. But it’s a good time and offers quite a few different modes to get acclimated and beat up famous faces."

"Right now, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a great version of a good retro game. Because the game was remade from the ground up, I wish the developers had made a super version of the Godzilla trilogy with more content. While Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered’s combat is really fun, there’s not much depth. There are lots of modes, and a bit of RPG unlocking, but this isn’t a deep fighting game that’s going to be played at tournaments. It’s a great budget buy for Godzilla fans. But more content would have made Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered a more obvious recommendation. If you’re at all curious, or have any fondness for the original game, it remains a fun time."

"In the media shadow of sacred monsters like Grand Theft Auto VI and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, only an equally fearless monstrosity could face them: Godzilla. Nearly a quarter century after its release on GameCube, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee returns with a remaster that discreetly refreshes the audiovisual experience and improves the progression without betraying its structure. The core is that of a 3D fighting game in which kaiju clashes are accompanied by the destruction of entire cities, in a blaze of explosions and particle effects. Behind this chaos lies a combat system that's immediate, but not always precise and balanced, suspended somewhere between classic fighting games and the festive jumble of a party game. The mechanics are simple, despite a certain unwieldiness in the movements, and the best of the action is found especially in local multiplayer."

Well, there you have it, folks! Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is an almost perfect example of a good '7' rated game. At the time of writing, the remaster is holding down a 72 score on Metacritic.

What's interesting is that the original Xbox release scored 73 on Metacritic - a single point higher than the remaster. It's funny how 23 years can pass and a game can be reviewed almost identically.
